He answered, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and with all your mind; and your neighbor as yourself.”
points.apply: Do one act of love for God and one for your neighbour today.

sub: The priest and Levite pass by; the Samaritan is moved with pity.
Mercy costs time, effort and money.
q: For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.
He said, “The one who showed him mercy.” Jesus said to him, “Go and do likewise.”
points.apply: Give time to someone others pass by.

sub: The Fathers saw the inn as the Church and the Samaritan as Christ.
Every parish is meant to care for the wounded.
q: He has told you, O mortal, what is good; and what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?
Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest.
points.apply: Welcome a newcomer or migrant worker in your parish.

concl: The Samaritan is Christ; the inn is the Church; the road to Jericho is ours.
Go and do likewise.
2026-11-07.resolve: Visit or phone someone lonely this week.

intro: Theme: “On this rock.”
Christ the head of the Church; Peter the rock of unity.

sub: God promised a precious cornerstone in Zion.
Christ is that stone, and the head of the body.
q: See, I am laying in Zion a foundation stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation: “One who trusts will not panic.”
Simon Peter answered, “You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.”
points.apply: Make Christ the first thought of your day.

sub: Faith is a gift, not a human achievement.
We ask the Father to deepen our faith.
q: The stone that the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone.
And Jesus answered him, “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah! For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father in heaven.”
points.apply: Pray for the gift of deeper faith.

sub: Christ builds; the gates of Hades will not prevail.
Communion with Peter's successor keeps the Church one.
q: Therefore thus says the Lord GOD, See, I am laying in Zion a foundation stone.
And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.
points.apply: Pray for the Pope and our Major Archbishop.

concl: Christ is the head; Peter's faith is the rock.
Let us stand firm in that faith.
2026-11-09.resolve: Pray the Creed slowly each day this week.

intro: Theme: “Listen to him.”
Peter's eyewitness memory of the Transfiguration.

sub: Moses' face shone after speaking with God.
Jesus' face changes as he prays.
q: Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone because he had been talking with God.
And while he was praying, the appearance of his face changed, and his clothes became dazzling white.
points.apply: Give ten minutes to silent prayer.

sub: The psalmist longs to see God's face.
In Jesus the face of God shines on us.
q: “Come,” my heart says, “seek his face!” Your face, LORD, do I seek.
Then from the cloud came a voice that said, “This is my Son, my Chosen; listen to him!”
points.apply: Read the Gospel slowly and keep one phrase.

sub: The prophetic word is a lamp until the day dawns.
The Church waits for the Morning Star.
q: The LORD make his face to shine upon you, and be gracious to you.
Jesus said to him, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.”
points.apply: Bless your family with Numbers 6:24–26 tonight.

concl: The glory of the mountain is the promise of our future.
Let us listen to the Son.
2026-11-10.resolve: Read one Gospel passage daily this week.

intro: Theme: “The wedding of the Lamb.”
The Bible ends with a wedding; the parable warns us to accept the invitation and wear the garment of grace.

sub: The prophets describe God as a Bridegroom.
Christ loves the Church as his Bride.
q: For as a young man marries a young woman, so shall your builder marry you, and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you.
Let us rejoice and exult and give him the glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his bride has made herself ready.
points.apply: Thank God for loving you as a Bridegroom.

sub: Isaiah sees a banquet for all nations.
The king's servants go to the streets.
q: On this mountain the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wines.
Go therefore into the main streets, and invite everyone you find to the wedding banquet.
points.apply: Invite someone to come with you to the Qurbana.

sub: The garment is the grace of baptism.
Keep it clean through confession.
q: And I will take you for my wife forever; I will take you for my wife in righteousness and in justice, in steadfast love and in mercy.
And the angel said to me, “Write this: Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.”
points.apply: Plan a good confession.

concl: The feast is ready; the invitation is ours.
Let us come, clothed in grace.
2026-11-11.resolve: Attend one weekday Qurbana this week.

intro: Theme: “The friend of the Bridegroom.”
Paul and John the Baptist both bring the bride to Christ and step aside with joy.

sub: God remembers Israel's first love in the desert.
The Church is called to that faithful love.
q: I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride, how you followed me in the wilderness, in a land not sown.
He who has the bride is the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice.
points.apply: Renew your first love for Christ in prayer.

sub: God takes his people as bride in faithfulness.
Paul guards the Church from “another Jesus”.
q: I will take you for my wife in faithfulness; and you shall know the LORD.
For this reason my joy has been fulfilled.
points.apply: Hold fast to the faith of the Church.

sub: John rejoices to step aside.
Every Christian points to Christ.
q: Not to us, O LORD, not to us, but to your name give glory.
He must increase, but I must decrease.
points.apply: Let someone else have the credit today.

concl: The Church belongs to Christ alone.
Let us rejoice to hear the Bridegroom's voice.
2026-11-12.resolve: Pray each morning this week: “Lord, you must increase.”

intro: Theme: “All things in his hands.”
Paul's vision makes him humble; Jesus, who comes from above, gives eternal life to those who believe.

points.h: No one sees God and lives
sub: Even Moses could not see God's face.
The Son who comes from above makes him known.
q: “You cannot see my face; for no one shall see me and live.”
The Father loves the Son and has placed all things in his hands.
points.apply: Thank Jesus for revealing the Father.

sub: Paul boasts only of weakness.
God's gifts are not trophies but trusts.
q: But I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with its mother.
He must increase, but I must decrease.
points.apply: Admit one weakness honestly to God.

sub: Faith in the Son is eternal life now.
Refusing the Son is refusing life.
q: The LORD make his face to shine upon you, and be gracious to you.
Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever disobeys the Son will not see life, but must endure God's wrath.
points.apply: Make an act of faith at midday.

concl: Heaven came down to us in the Son.
Let us place all things in his hands.
2026-11-13.resolve: Pray “Jesus, I trust in you” whenever you are anxious this week.

intro: Theme: “Like children, toward the river of life.”
The vision of the heavenly city and Jesus' welcome to the little ones.

sub: Ezekiel saw a river from the Temple bringing life and healing.
Revelation shows it flowing from the throne of God and the Lamb.
q: Their leaves will not wither nor their fruit fail, but they will bear fresh fruit every month, because the water for them flows from the sanctuary. Their fruit will be for food, and their leaves for healing.
Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb.
points.apply: Thank God for the grace that flows from the sacraments.

sub: The longing of every psalm is fulfilled.
There will be no more night.
q: “Come,” my heart says, “seek his face!” Your face, LORD, do I seek.
They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. And there will be no more night.
points.apply: End the day with a prayer of longing for heaven.

points.h: The Kingdom belongs to the little ones
sub: God's praise comes from the mouths of infants.
Jesus welcomes children; so must we.
q: Out of the mouths of babes and infants you have founded a bulwark because of your foes.
But Jesus said, “Let the little children come to me, and do not stop them; for it is to such as these that the kingdom of heaven belongs.”
points.apply: Pray with the children in your family tonight.

concl: The journey of the Church ends at the river of life.
Let us go there as children.
2026-11-14.resolve: Teach a child one short prayer this week.

intro: Theme: “The greatest is love.”
Jesus joins the two great commandments; Paul paints love's portrait.

sub: The Shema is Israel's daily prayer.
Love of God involves the whole person.
q: Hear, O Israel: The LORD is our God, the LORD alone. You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your might.

Jesus answered, “The first is, ‘Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one; you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength.’”
points.apply: Pray the Shema slowly this morning.

sub: The second commandment is like the first.
No sacrifice replaces love.
q: You shall not take vengeance or bear a grudge against any of your people, but you shall love your neighbor as yourself: I am the LORD.
The second is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no other commandment greater than these.
points.apply: Forgive one grudge today.

sub: Love gives meaning to worship.
The Qurbana is love's sacrifice.
q: For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.

And ‘to love him with all the heart, and with all the understanding, and with all the strength,’ and ‘to love one's neighbor as oneself,’—this is much more important than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.
points.apply: Come to the Qurbana reconciled with others.

concl: Love is the first and greatest commandment.
Without it we are nothing; with it we are near the Kingdom.
2026-11-16.resolve: Read 1 Corinthians 13 each evening this week.

intro: Theme: “Trustworthy stewards.”
Paul's stewards of the mysteries and Jesus' shrewd manager teach the right use of what is entrusted to us.

points.h: Honour the Lord with your wealth
sub: All we have comes from God.
Giving the first fruits shows whom we trust.
q: Honor the LORD with your substance and with the first fruits of all your produce.
And I tell you, make friends for yourselves by means of dishonest wealth so that when it is gone, they may welcome you into the eternal homes.
points.apply: Set aside a fixed part of your income for the poor.

sub: Small honesty prepares great faithfulness.
God sees the small things.
q: You shall have only a full and honest weight; you shall have only a full and honest measure.
Whoever is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much; and whoever is dishonest in a very little is dishonest also in much.
points.apply: Correct one small dishonesty today.

sub: Money is a good servant and a bad master.
We are free when God alone is Lord.
q: Hear, O Israel: The LORD is our God, the LORD alone.
No slave can serve two masters; for a slave will either hate the one and love the other, or be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and wealth.
points.apply: Fast from one unnecessary purchase this week.

concl: We are stewards of God's gifts and mysteries.
Let us be found trustworthy.
2026-11-17.resolve: Review your spending this week in the light of the Gospel.

intro: Theme: “Washed, and called to enter.”
Baptism gives a new identity; the Kingdom asks for resolve.

sub: God promised to cleanse his people and give a new spirit.
Baptism fulfils that promise.
q: I will put my spirit within you, and you shall live.
Jesus answered, “Very truly, I tell you, no one can enter the kingdom of God without being born of water and Spirit.”
points.apply: Thank God for your baptism today.

sub: Paul reminds the Corinthians who they now are.
Sin contradicts our baptismal identity.
q: You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy.
So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: everything old has passed away; see, everything has become new!
points.apply: Renounce one old habit that contradicts your baptism.

sub: Grace makes effort possible.
No one can serve two masters.
q: Choose this day whom you will serve… but as for me and my household, we will serve the LORD.
The law and the prophets were in effect until John came; since then the good news of the kingdom of God is proclaimed, and everyone tries to enter it by force.
points.apply: Cut off one occasion of sin today.

concl: We were washed; now we walk in newness of life.
Let us enter the Kingdom with all our heart.
2026-11-18.resolve: Renew your baptismal promises at night prayer this week.

intro: Theme: “Good soil.”
The Gospel grows in the world; the sower's seed bears fruit in hearts that hear.

points.h: The word does not return empty
sub: God's word always accomplishes its purpose.
The Gospel is bearing fruit worldwide.
q: So shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose.
But blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear.
points.apply: Thank God for those who sowed the word in you.

sub: Isaiah warned of ears that hear but do not understand.
Hardness and worry choke the seed.
q: Keep listening, but do not comprehend; keep looking, but do not understand.
As for what was sown among thorns, this is the one who hears the word, but the cares of the world and the lure of wealth choke the word, and it yields nothing.
points.apply: Name one worry and give it to God.

sub: Good soil hears, understands and keeps.
Fruit is seen in good works.
q: They are like trees planted by streams of water, which yield their fruit in its season.
But as for what was sown on good soil, this is the one who hears the word and understands it, who indeed bears fruit and yields, in one case a hundredfold, in another sixty, and in another thirty.
points.apply: Read tomorrow's Gospel tonight.

concl: The seed is good; let the soil be good.
Blessed are the ears that hear.
2026-11-19.resolve: Give ten minutes to the word of God every day this week.

intro: Theme: “Pruned to bear more fruit.”
Discipline from the Father's love and the vine that gives life to the branches.

points.h: The Lord reproves the one he loves
sub: Discipline is a sign of sonship.
It yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness.
q: My child, do not despise the LORD's discipline or be weary of his reproof, for the LORD reproves the one he loves, as a father the son in whom he delights.
He removes every branch in me that bears no fruit. Every branch that bears fruit he prunes to make it bear more fruit.
points.apply: Offer one present difficulty to God as his pruning.

sub: Israel was God's vine brought out of Egypt.
Jesus is the true vine; we are his branches.
q: You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it.
I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinegrower.
points.apply: Thank God for being grafted into Christ by baptism.

sub: Without him we can do nothing.
Fruit glorifies the Father.
q: Let me sing for my beloved my love-song concerning his vineyard: My beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill.
My Father is glorified by this, that you bear much fruit and become my disciples.
points.apply: Visit the Blessed Sacrament today.

concl: The Father prunes in love; the Son gives life.
Let us abide in him and bear fruit.
2026-11-20.resolve: Begin each day this week with: “Lord, without you I can do nothing.”

intro: Theme: “Our Father in faith brought us the Way.”
The Syro-Malabar Church remembers the entrance of St Thomas into India (tradition: AD 52, Kodungallur) and the Presentation of Mary.

points.h: Called and sent with a promise
sub: God sends Moses with the promise of freedom.
God chooses his servant from the ends of the earth: “Do not fear.”
Thomas was sent to the ends of the earth, and came to us.
q: You whom I took from the ends of the earth, and called from its farthest corners, saying to you, “You are my servant, I have chosen you and not cast you off”; do not fear, for I am with you.
Jesus said to them again, “Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, so I send you.”
points.apply: Share your faith with one person who does not know Christ.

sub: The Gentiles become members of God's household.
The Church is built on the foundation of the apostles.
India's Christians are built on the faith of Thomas.
q: I will take you as my people, and I will be your God.

So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are citizens with the saints and also members of the household of God, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone.
points.apply: Pray for the Syro-Malabar Church and all St Thomas Christians.

sub: Thomas asks how to know the way; Jesus is the Way.
Our ancestors called the faith “Margam”.
Thomas's confession is ours at every Qurbana.
q: Do not fear, for I am with you, do not be afraid, for I am your God; I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you with my victorious right hand.
Thomas said to him, “Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?” Jesus said to him, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.”
points.apply: Say “My Lord and my God” at the elevation at every Qurbana.

concl: Thomas brought us not an idea but a Person.
Let us walk the Way and bring others to it.
2026-11-21.resolve: Learn and tell your children the story of St Thomas in India.

intro: Theme: “The Way to the Father's house.”
The promise of many dwelling places and access to the Father in one Spirit.

sub: Jesus speaks peace before his Passion.
Faith in God and in Christ calms the heart.
q: As a mother comforts her child, so I will comfort you.
Do not let your hearts be troubled. Believe in God, believe also in me.
points.apply: Hand over one anxiety to Jesus each time it returns.

sub: Thomas asks; Jesus answers.
No one comes to the Father except through him.
q: The LORD make his face to shine upon you, and be gracious to you.
Jesus said to him, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.”
points.apply: Pray: “Jesus, show me the way today.”

sub: Jesus reveals the Father's face.
In Christ, God dwells among us.
q: Sing and rejoice, O daughter Zion! For lo, I will come and dwell in your midst, says the LORD.
Jesus said to him, “Have I been with you all this time, Philip, and you still do not know me? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.”
points.apply: Spend five minutes looking at a crucifix and seeing the Father's love.

concl: The Father's house has a room for each of us.
Jesus is the Way there.
2026-11-23.resolve: Pray John 14:1–6 each morning this week.

intro: Theme: “One flock, one Shepherd.”
A chosen people and the Good Shepherd who gathers all.

sub: At Sinai God called Israel a priestly kingdom.
Peter gives this dignity to the baptised.
q: But you shall be for me a priestly kingdom and a holy nation.
I am the gate. Whoever enters by me will be saved, and will come in and go out and find pasture.
points.apply: Offer your day as a priestly sacrifice.

sub: The thief destroys; the Shepherd gives life.
He lays down his life for the sheep.
q: He will feed his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arms.
The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life, and have it abundantly. I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
points.apply: Name one “thief” that steals your peace and refuse it.

sub: God promised one shepherd for his people.
Christ desires the unity of all.
q: My servant David shall be king over them; and they shall all have one shepherd.
So there will be one flock, one shepherd.
points.apply: Pray for Christian unity today.

concl: We are God's own people, gathered by the Shepherd.
Let us listen to his voice and pray for one flock.
2026-11-24.resolve: Pray Jesus' prayer for unity (John 17:21) daily this week.

intro: Theme: “He has done great things.”
Paul's hymn of God's plan and Mary's Magnificat close the year in praise.

sub: God chose us before the foundation of the world.
His plan is to gather all things in Christ.
q: And in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.
His mercy is for those who fear him from generation to generation.
points.apply: Thank God for three blessings of this year.

sub: Hannah sang it before Mary.
God reverses the world's order.
q: The LORD makes poor and makes rich; he brings low, he also exalts. He raises up the poor from the dust; he lifts the needy from the ash heap.
He has brought down the powerful from their thrones, and lifted up the lowly; he has filled the hungry with good things.
points.apply: Do one act of respect for someone overlooked.

sub: Mary is the first of the redeemed.
The Church is called to her humility and praise.
q: Happy is the nation whose God is the LORD, the people whom he has chosen as his heritage.
For he has looked with favor on the lowliness of his servant… for the Mighty One has done great things for me.
points.apply: Pray the Magnificat tonight.

concl: The year ends in praise.
With Mary we sing: holy is his name.
2026-11-25.resolve: Pray the Magnificat each evening until Annunciation Sunday.

intro: Theme: “Names written in heaven.”
Pilgrims without a lasting city, rejoicing that they belong to God.

sub: Abraham lived in tents looking for the city with foundations.
The Church walks toward the heavenly city.
q: Then Jacob woke from his sleep and said, “Surely the LORD is in this place—and I did not know it!”
Nevertheless, do not rejoice at this, that the spirits submit to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.
points.apply: Hold possessions lightly today.

sub: Jesus rejoices in the Spirit.
He thanks the Father for the little ones.
q: As a mother comforts her child, so I will comfort you.

At that same hour Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and the intelligent and have revealed them to infants.”
points.apply: Thank God for one simple person who taught you faith.

sub: Praise and sharing are the Christian's sacrifices.
The Qurbana is the great sacrifice of praise.
q: For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is great among the nations, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure offering.
He said to them, “I watched Satan fall from heaven like a flash of lightning.”
points.apply: Praise God aloud for five minutes today.

concl: Our joy is that God knows our names.
Let us praise him and share with others.
2026-11-26.resolve: End each day this week with a prayer of praise.

intro: Theme: “The God of the living.”
Jesus defends the resurrection; John sees the great multitude before the Lamb.

points.h: The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
sub: God revealed himself to Moses by the names of the patriarchs.
They live to him.
q: He said further, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” And Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God.

And as for the dead being raised, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the story about the bush, how God said to him, ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is God not of the dead, but of the living.
points.apply: Pray for your ancestors in faith.

sub: The Church is catholic: every tribe and language.
Salvation belongs to God and the Lamb.
q: In days to come… all the nations shall stream to it.

After this I looked, and there was a great multitude that no one could count, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, robed in white, with palm branches in their hands.
points.apply: Pray for Christians of another nation today.

sub: Heaven's liturgy is praise.
Our Qurbana joins it.
q: For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is great among the nations.
Singing, “Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and might be to our God forever and ever! Amen.”
points.apply: Sing a hymn of praise at family prayer tonight.

concl: God is the God of the living; our hope is the resurrection.
The Church's end is eternal praise.
2026-11-27.resolve: Pray the Creed slowly each day this week.

intro: Theme: “We have found the Messiah.”
The last day of the year: the heavenly temple, worship in spirit and truth, and St Andrew who brings others to Jesus.

sub: Jacob finds God in an unexpected place.
Every church is a gate of heaven.
q: And he was afraid, and said, “How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.”
I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb.
points.apply: Enter church tomorrow with reverence.

sub: Andrew and Peter leave their nets at once.
Discipleship begins with a decision.
q: I am now sending for many fishermen, says the LORD, and they shall catch them.
And he said to them, “Follow me, and I will make you fish for people.” Immediately they left their nets and followed him.
points.apply: Leave one “net” that holds you back.

sub: Andrew brings Peter.
The nations will say: “Let us go with you, for God is with you.”
q: In those days ten men from nations of every language shall take hold of a Jew, grasping his garment and saying, “Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.”
He first found his brother Simon and said to him, “We have found the Messiah.”
points.apply: Invite someone to the Qurbana tomorrow.

concl: The year ends where it began: with the house of God.
Tomorrow a new year begins; bring someone with you.
2026-11-28.resolve: Begin the new liturgical year with confession and Holy Qurbana.

intro: Theme: “The righteous live by faith.”
Abraham's faith brings blessing; Jesus heals where the disciples failed.

sub: Faith was reckoned to Abraham as righteousness.
Believers are Abraham's children.
q: And he believed the LORD; and the LORD reckoned it to him as righteousness.
For this reason, those who believe are blessed with Abraham who believed.
points.apply: Make an act of faith each morning this week.

sub: The prophet Habakkuk: the righteous live by faith.
Christ bore the curse so that the blessing might reach us.
q: Look at the proud! Their spirit is not right in them, but the righteous live by their faith.
In order that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.
points.apply: Thank Christ for bearing the curse for you.

sub: The disciples could not heal.
Jesus restores the boy to his father.
q: Is anything too wonderful for the LORD?
Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. And all were astounded at the greatness of God.
points.apply: Bring one impossible situation to Jesus.

concl: Faith receives what God promises.
Let us trust the One who heals.
2026-11-30.resolve: Pray “Lord, increase my faith” daily during this season.

lead: Qudash Edtha, the last season of the East Syriac year, looks at the Church as God's dwelling and as the bride waiting for her Lord. Today's readings follow the place where God meets his people. In Exodus it is a tent pitched outside a sinful camp. In Isaiah, God himself is the strength of a tired people in exile. In Hebrews, Christ enters the true tent, not made with hands, with his own blood. In Matthew the door of the wedding hall opens for those who are ready. The line runs from a tent of meeting to a wedding feast, and its key words are meeting, waiting and entering.

r.h: The tent outside the camp
set: The chapter comes straight after the golden calf (Exodus 32). God still promises the land, but says he will not go up among the people, "or I would consume you on the way, for you are a stiff-necked people" (33:3). The people mourn and take off their ornaments at Horeb (33:4–6). The question of the whole chapter is whether God will still live among a people who have sinned.
str: vv. 1–3: the promise renewed, and God's refusal to go "among" them.
vv. 4–6: the people's mourning and the stripping of ornaments.
vv. 7–11: a description of what Moses used to do with the tent of meeting.

¶ In vv. 7–11 the Hebrew verbs describe a repeated custom, not a single event, so the NRSV rightly says "Moses used to take the tent". This tent is not yet the great Tabernacle of chapters 35–40. It is a simpler meeting place, and it stands outside the camp.
kw: Mô‘ēd comes from a verb meaning to fix a time or place, to meet by appointment. The tent is the place where God keeps an appointment with his people.
The cloud that led Israel out of Egypt (13:21) now comes down to the door of the tent. Jewish tradition later called this dwelling presence the Shekinah.
An idiom of closeness and directness, like Numbers 12:8, "mouth to mouth". It does not mean that Moses saw God's essence: a few verses later God says, "you cannot see my face" (33:20).
vv: And everyone who sought the Lord would go out to the tent of meeting, which was outside the camp.
To seek the Lord, the people have to leave the camp, the place where the calf was made. Worship begins with a going out.
When Moses entered the tent, the pillar of cloud would descend and stand at the entrance of the tent, and the Lord would speak with Moses.
The people do not enter, but they see the cloud and bow down, each at the door of his own tent (33:10). One man's prayer becomes the worship of the whole people.
Thus the Lord used to speak to Moses face to face, as one speaks to a friend.

This is the high point of the passage. After the worst sin of the desert, God speaks with a man as a friend. The verse ends with Joshua, the young assistant, who "would not leave the tent". The man who will lead Israel into the land learns first to stay in God's presence. His name, Yehoshua, is the same name as Jesus.
ch: The Catechism takes Exodus 33:11 as the model of Moses' prayer of intercession, a friend speaking with a friend (CCC 2574–2577). The Letter to the Hebrews sees Jesus as the one who "suffered outside the city gate", and invites us: "Let us then go to him outside the camp" (Hebrews 13:12–13). St Gregory of Nyssa ends his Life of Moses by saying that the goal of the whole spiritual life is to become, like Moses, a friend of God (in substance).

r.h: Those who wait for the Lord
set: Chapters 40–55 of Isaiah, often called the Book of Consolation, speak to the Jews in exile in Babylon, in the years before Cyrus allowed them to return (539 BC). They open with "Comfort, O comfort my people" (40:1). The exiles live among the great temples and star-gods of Babylon and wonder whether their own God has forgotten them.
str: v. 20: a satire on idols. A poor man chooses wood that will not rot and hires a craftsman so that his god will not fall over.
vv. 21–24: the Creator who "sits above the circle of the earth" and brings rulers to nothing.
vv. 25–26: "To whom then will you compare me?" God calls the stars by name. In Babylon the stars were gods; here they are soldiers on parade, counted by their Maker.
v. 27: Israel's complaint: "My way is hidden from the Lord."
vv. 28–31: God's answer.
kw: those who wait for the Lord (v. 31)

The verb qāwāh means to wait with eager hope. It is related to qaw, a cord or rope. Hope here is something stretched tight toward God, not idle waiting. The Malayalam POC translates "those who trust in God", which brings out the same attitude from another side.
Literally "they shall exchange strength". The tired give God their weakness and receive his strength.
The same image as Exodus 19:4: "I bore you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself." The God of the Exodus will carry his people a second time.
vv: The Lord is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth. He does not faint or grow weary; his understanding is unsearchable.
He gives power to the faint, and strengthens the powerless.
but those who wait for the Lord shall renew their strength, they shall mount up with wings like eagles, they shall run and not be weary, they shall walk and not faint.

The order of the last line is surprising: fly, run, walk. It seems to go downward, but that is the point. Flying is the rare moment of joy, running is the time of effort, and walking is ordinary daily life. God's strength is given for the long, plain walk most of all.
ch: The Catechism defines hope as the virtue by which we desire the Kingdom and eternal life, "placing our trust in Christ's promises and relying not on our own strength, but on the help of the grace of the Holy Spirit" (CCC 1817). Isaiah 40 is the Old Testament school of that virtue. On a Sunday of Qudash Edtha it reminds a tired Church that her strength comes from the God she waits for.

r.h: Christ entered the tent not made with hands
set: Hebrews calls itself "a word of exhortation" (13:22). It is a sermon written to Christians, probably of Jewish background, who were growing tired and were tempted to drift back. Its author is not named; the Church received it among the letters linked with St Paul. Chapters 7–10 present Christ as the high priest of a new covenant.
str: vv. 1–5: the earthly tent and its furnishings: lampstand, table, bread, the Holy of Holies with the ark.
vv. 6–7: the priests enter the first room every day; the high priest enters the inner room only once a year, with blood, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16).
vv. 8–10: the lesson the Holy Spirit gives: the way into the sanctuary was not yet open. The old tent was "a symbol of the present time".
vv. 11–12: Christ's entry.
vv. 13–14: an argument from the lesser to the greater: "how much more".
kw: The same word the Greek Old Testament uses for the tent of Exodus. Today's first reading and epistle speak of the same reality: the place where God and his people meet.
See also Mark 14:58 and 2 Corinthians 5:1. The true sanctuary is the heavenly one, and Christ's own risen body.
The high priest had to return every year. Christ's sacrifice is never repeated, because it is complete.
Lytron is the price paid to set a slave or a captive free (compare Mark 10:45).
The word for liturgical service. The purpose of redemption is that we may worship the living God.
vv: But when Christ came as a high priest of the good things that have come, then through the greater and perfect tent (not made with hands, that is, not of this creation), he entered once for all into the Holy Place, not with the blood of goats and calves, but with his own blood, thus obtaining eternal redemption.

A note on the text. In v. 11 the ancient manuscripts differ. Some of the oldest (the papyrus P46 and Codex Vaticanus) read "the good things that have come", which the NRSV follows. Many others, and the Latin Vulgate, read "the good things to come", which the Malayalam POC follows (വരാനിരിക്കുന്ന നൻമകളുടെ). Both readings are true to the faith: in Christ the good things have already come, and their fullness is still to come.
how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to worship the living God!

Most of the Fathers understood "the eternal Spirit" as the Holy Spirit: the whole Trinity is at work in the Cross. The Son offers, the Spirit is the fire of the offering, and the Father receives it. The result is a cleansed conscience and true worship.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ "entered into heaven itself" as our high priest (CCC 662), and that the Eucharist makes present the one sacrifice of the Cross, not another sacrifice (CCC 1366–1367). St John Chrysostom, preaching on Hebrews, says that we do not offer another sacrifice each day, but always the same one (in substance). This is what happens at every Holy Qurbana: the Church on earth joins the one offering of Christ in the true sanctuary.

r.h: Those who were ready went in
set: This parable belongs to Jesus' last great discourse, about the end of the age (Matthew 24–25). Three parables close it: the ten bridesmaids (readiness), the talents (faithful work) and the judgment of the nations (love for the least). Matthew writes for a Church that knows the Lord's return may be delayed.

In a Palestinian wedding of that time, the bridegroom went to the bride's family home and then brought her in procession to his own house, often at night. Friends went out with lights to meet the procession and enter the feast with it. The "lamps" were probably torches, rags soaked in oil on a stick, which burned out quickly and needed fresh oil.
str: vv. 1–4: ten bridesmaids, five wise and five foolish. The difference is the flask of oil.
v. 5: the bridegroom is delayed, and all of them sleep.
v. 6: the cry at midnight.
vv. 7–9: "our lamps are going out"; the oil cannot be shared.
v. 10: those who were ready go in, and the door is shut.
vv. 11–12: "Lord, lord, open to us." "I do not know you."
v. 13: the lesson: keep awake.
kw: The same pair as the house on the rock and the house on the sand (7:24–27). Wisdom in Matthew means hearing Jesus' word and doing it.
The parable expects a delay. The test is not a short burst of fervour but faithfulness over a long night.
The word used for going out to welcome an important visitor. Paul uses a related word for the Church meeting the Lord at his coming (1 Thessalonians 4:17).
vv: As the bridegroom was delayed, all of them became drowsy and slept.
The wise sleep too. Sleep is not the fault; we are human and the night is long. The fault is to have no oil when the cry comes.
And while they went to buy it, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went with him into the wedding banquet; and the door was shut.
The refusal to share (v. 9) is not meanness. The parable teaches that some things cannot be borrowed at the last moment: a life of faith and love is personal.
But he replied, ‘Truly I tell you, I do not know you.’

In the Bible, to "know" someone means a relationship, not information. The words echo 7:23: "I never knew you." The door is shut not because the bridegroom is harsh, but because there was no relationship to open it.
Keep awake therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour.
ch: Many Fathers saw the oil as charity and good works, which give light to faith; so St Augustine and St John Chrysostom (in substance). St Jerome records an old tradition that the Lord would return at midnight, which he connects with the custom of keeping the Easter vigil until midnight (in substance). The Catechism quotes the Second Vatican Council: since we know neither the day nor the hour, we must, as the Lord advised, watch constantly (CCC 1036; Lumen Gentium 48). The Church is the bride going out to meet the bridegroom (CCC 796).

qa: Did Moses see God's face or not?
"Face to face" (33:11) is an idiom for friendship and directness. Seeing God's essence is reserved for heaven (33:20; 1 Corinthians 13:12). In Christ we see the face of the Father (John 14:9).
Why did the wise bridesmaids refuse to share?
The parable is not about lending. Readiness for Christ is something each person must have; no one else can supply it at the last moment.
Does Hebrews say the old worship was worthless?
No. It calls the old tent a "symbol" and a teacher that pointed to Christ (9:8–10). The Church honours the covenant with Israel, which God never revoked (CCC 121, 839).
rite: On the first Sunday of Qudash Edtha the Church looks at herself as the tent of meeting and the bride. The church building, consecrated with holy oil, is our tent of meeting; the Holy Qurbana is our entry, with Christ, into the sanctuary not made with hands; and the season points to the wedding feast at the end of time. The oil of the bridesmaids may remind us of the oil of baptism and chrism, which must be kept burning by prayer and love.
study: In Exodus 33, the people must go out of the camp to seek the Lord. What do I need to leave behind to go to him?
Isaiah 40:31 moves from flying to walking. Where do I most need strength for the plain, daily walk?
Hebrews 9:14 says Christ's blood cleanses the conscience "to worship the living God". How does this change the way I take part in the Holy Qurbana?
What is the "oil" in my lamp, and how do I keep it from running out?

lead: On the first Monday of Qudash Edtha the Church keeps the commemoration of all the faithful departed. The season looks at the Church as God's house, and today we remember that this house has rooms beyond the grave: the Church on earth, the Church being purified, and the Church in glory are one family (CCC 954). The four readings move from a valley of dry bones to an open tomb. In Ezekiel, God's breath raises a dead people. In 2 Maccabees, Judas prays and offers sacrifice for fallen soldiers, "taking account of the resurrection". In 1 Corinthians, Paul sings that death is swallowed up in victory. In John, Jesus tells Martha, "I am the resurrection and the life." The key words are breath, prayer, victory and life.

r.h: Can these bones live?
set: Ezekiel was a priest who was taken to Babylon with the first group of exiles in 597 BC (1:1–3). When Jerusalem and the Temple fell in 587 BC, the exiles felt that their story was over. They said, "Our bones are dried up, and our hope is lost" (37:11). From chapter 33 the book turns from judgment to hope: God promises a new heart and a new spirit (36:26–27), then gives this vision, and finally shows the prophet a new Temple (chapters 40–48).
str: vv. 1–2: the valley full of very dry bones.
v. 3: God's question and the prophet's answer.
vv. 4–6: the command to prophesy to the bones.
vv. 7–8: the bones come together and are covered with flesh, "but there was no breath in them".
vv. 9–10: the prophet speaks to the breath, and a vast multitude stands up.
vv. 11–14: God explains the vision: the bones are the whole house of Israel; God will open their graves and put his spirit within them.
¶ The vision happens in two stages, like the making of the first man in Genesis 2:7: first the body is shaped, then God gives the breath of life. The return from exile is pictured as a new creation.
kw: One Hebrew word runs through the whole passage, and the NRSV has to translate it in three ways: "the spirit of the Lord" (v. 1), "breath" (vv. 5–10), "the four winds" (v. 9), and "my spirit" (v. 14). The wind that blows, the breath that gives life and the Spirit of God are one image.

God's usual name for Ezekiel, used more than ninety times in the book. It reminds the prophet that he is a weak creature standing before the living God. The Malayalam POC keeps the literal form, "son of man".
In v. 12 the picture changes from a battlefield to a cemetery. The God who opens graves is stronger than the place where every human story seems to end.
vv: He said to me, “Mortal, can these bones live?” I answered, “O Lord God, you know.”
The prophet does not say yes, because the bones are very dry. He does not say no, because he is speaking to God. His answer is the beginning of faith: what is impossible for us is known to God.
I prophesied as he commanded me, and the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood on their feet, a vast multitude.
The word of God, spoken by a man, brings life. This is a picture of preaching in the Church: the minister speaks, but the life comes from the breath of God.
I will put my spirit within you, and you shall live, and I will place you on your own soil

In its first meaning the vision promises the return of the exiles to their land (v. 12). But the image of graves opened by God prepares the clear faith in the resurrection of the body found later in Daniel 12:2 and in 2 Maccabees 7.
ch: St Irenaeus, in Against Heresies, and Tertullian, in On the Resurrection of the Flesh, read this vision as a promise that God will raise our bodies (in substance). The Catechism teaches that God revealed the resurrection of the dead to his people step by step (CCC 992), and that the righteous will live for ever with the risen Christ (CCC 989). The Roman Rite reads this passage at the Vigil of Pentecost, because the breath of Ezekiel is fulfilled in the Holy Spirit, whom the Creed calls "the Lord, the giver of life".

r.h: Praying for the dead
set: 2 Maccabees tells of the Jewish struggle for faith under the Syrian king Antiochus IV Epiphanes and of the revolt led by Judas Maccabeus (about 167–160 BC). The author says that his book is a summary of a five-volume history by Jason of Cyrene (2:23). It was written in Greek and belongs to the books which the Church received with the Greek Old Testament, called deuterocanonical. The Council of Trent confirmed them as part of Holy Scripture.
After a battle against Gorgias, the governor of Idumea (12:32–37), Judas goes back to bury his fallen soldiers.
str: v. 38: the army keeps the sabbath at Adullam.
v. 39: Judas and his men go to bring back the bodies for burial with their families.
v. 40: under the tunics of the dead they find tokens of the idols of Jamnia, forbidden by the law.
vv. 41–42: they bless God, the just judge, and pray that the sin may be blotted out; Judas warns the living to keep away from sin.
v. 43: a collection is sent to Jerusalem for a sin offering.
vv. 44–45: the author explains: this was done because of faith in the resurrection.
kw: The word the New Testament uses for the resurrection of Jesus. Here, more than a century and a half before Christ, the author says plainly that the dead "would rise again" (v. 44).
Yavneh, a town on the coastal plain west of Judea, with its own pagan cult. The soldiers seem to have carried its tokens as charms for protection in battle.
A Greek silver coin. Two thousand drachmas was a large sum, gathered "man by man" (v. 43): the whole army took part in the prayer for its dead.
vv: and they turned to supplication, praying that the sin that had been committed might be wholly blotted out.

The soldiers had died in a serious fault, yet they had died fighting for God's people. Judas does not judge their souls. He leaves them to "the righteous judge, who reveals the things that are hidden" (v. 41), and he prays.
For if he were not expecting that those who had fallen would rise again, it would have been superfluous and foolish to pray for the dead.
The author's logic is simple: we pray for the dead because they are not lost. Prayer for the dead is an act of faith in the resurrection.
Therefore he made atonement for the dead, so that they might be delivered from their sin.
Some Bibles, including the Latin Vulgate, number this sentence as 12:46. It is the text the Catechism cites when it teaches about the final purification.
ch: The Catechism quotes this passage when it speaks of purgatory, the final purification of those who die in God's grace and friendship but are still imperfectly purified (CCC 1030–1032). It teaches that from the beginning the Church has honoured the memory of the dead and offered prayers for them, above all the Eucharistic sacrifice (CCC 1032). St Augustine tells in his Confessions that his mother Monica, as she was dying, asked only one thing: to be remembered at the altar of the Lord wherever her sons might be (in substance).

r.h: Death has been swallowed up in victory
set: 1 Corinthians 15 is the longest New Testament chapter on the resurrection. Some in Corinth were saying "there is no resurrection of the dead" (15:12). Paul answers by recalling the creed he received, that Christ died, was buried and was raised (15:3–5). Christ is "the first fruits of those who have died" (15:20). Then Paul explains what the risen body is like: a seed is sown perishable and raised imperishable (15:42–44). Today's verses are the climax of the chapter.
str: v. 51: "a mystery": not all will die, but all will be changed.
v. 52: the moment of the change, at the last trumpet.
vv. 53–54: the perishable must put on imperishability.
vv. 54–55: two prophets fulfilled: Isaiah 25:8 and Hosea 13:14.
v. 56: the sting of death is sin.
v. 57: thanksgiving for the victory given in Christ.
v. 58: the practical conclusion: stand firm and keep working.
kw: In Paul, not a puzzle but a part of God's plan that was hidden and is now revealed.
The risen body is the same body, changed. Paul uses the picture of putting on a garment: the mortal body "puts on" immortality.
The sting of a scorpion or the goad used to drive an ox. Death is like a poisonous creature whose poison is sin. Christ has taken the poison out of it.
Paul repeats the word three times (vv. 54, 55, 57). The victory is not ours by nature; God "gives" it through Christ.
vv: We will not all die, but we will all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet.

A note on the text. The Greek says literally "we will not all sleep", the gentle Christian word for death. The ancient manuscripts differ a little here, and the Latin Vulgate reads "we shall all rise again, but we shall not all be changed". The NRSV and the Malayalam POC follow the reading of most Greek manuscripts. Paul means that those still alive at the Lord's coming will be changed without dying.
“Death has been swallowed up in victory.” “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?”
Isaiah 25:8 promised that on God's mountain he "will swallow up death forever". Hosea 13:14 was a cry of judgment; Paul turns it into a song of mockery against a defeated enemy.
Therefore, my beloved, be steadfast, immovable, always excelling in the work of the Lord, because you know that in the Lord your labor is not in vain.
The great chapter on the resurrection ends not with a dream but with work. Because the dead will rise, nothing done for the Lord is wasted.
ch: The Catechism follows Paul closely when it asks how the dead rise: the body will be raised incorruptible, and the "how" goes beyond our imagination and is open only to faith (CCC 999–1001). This passage is often read at Christian funerals. It tells mourners that the body laid in the grave is like a seed, and that the last word belongs to the God who gives the victory.

r.h: I am the resurrection and the life
set: The raising of Lazarus is the last and greatest of the signs in the first half of John's Gospel. It leads straight to the council's decision to put Jesus to death (11:45–53): the gift of life to Lazarus costs Jesus his own life. Bethany lay on the Mount of Olives, about three kilometres from Jerusalem ("some two miles", v. 18; POC "fifteen stadia").

Burial took place on the day of death, and mourning lasted seven days, with friends coming to console the family. A later Jewish tradition held that the soul stayed near the body for three days; after four days death was beyond doubt. "The Jews" in v. 19 are friends and neighbours from Judea who come to comfort the sisters; John presents them kindly here.
str: v. 17: Lazarus has been in the tomb four days.
vv. 18–19: Bethany, and the many who have come to console.
v. 20: Martha goes out to meet Jesus; Mary stays at home.
vv. 21–22: Martha's sorrow and her trust.
vv. 23–24: "Your brother will rise again", which Martha understands of the last day.
vv. 25–26: Jesus' revelation and his question.
v. 27: Martha's confession of faith.
kw: One of the seven great "I am" sayings in John (the bread of life, the light of the world, the gate, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life, the way, the truth and the life, the true vine). They echo the name of God revealed to Moses (Exodus 3:14).
Martha believes in a resurrection at the end of time. Jesus tells her that the resurrection is not only an event in the future; it is a person, present before her now.
John uses the verb "believe" close to a hundred times, but never the noun "faith". For John faith is always an action: a trust that moves toward a person.
vv: Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that God will give you whatever you ask of him.
Martha's words hold sorrow and trust together. She is not afraid to tell the Lord her pain, and she does not stop trusting him. This is the prayer of every grieving Christian.
I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live, and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?
Two promises: the believer who dies will live (the resurrection), and the believer who lives will never die (eternal life, which begins now). Bodily death remains, but it is no longer the end.
Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God, the one coming into the world.

Martha's confession is the fullest in the Gospel before Easter, and it is close to the purpose John gives for his whole book: "that you may come to believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God" (20:31). In Matthew a similar confession is made by Peter (Matthew 16:16).
ch: The Catechism quotes v. 25 when it teaches that Jesus links faith in the resurrection to his own person (CCC 994). St Augustine, preaching on the three dead whom Jesus raised in the Gospels, sees in Lazarus, four days in the tomb, the soul bound by a long habit of sin, and he teaches that even such a soul can be called out by the voice of Christ (in substance). This Gospel is read at many Christian funerals: at the grave the Church repeats Martha's faith.

qa: Is praying for the dead found in the Bible?

Yes. 2 Maccabees 12 praises Judas for praying and offering sacrifice for the dead. Many scholars also think that Onesiphorus, for whom Paul prays in 2 Timothy 1:16–18, had already died. The Church has prayed for the dead from the beginning, above all in the Eucharist (CCC 958, 1032).
What is purgatory? Is it a second chance?

No. Purgatory is not a second chance for those who rejected God. It is the final purification of those who die in God's grace and friendship but are still imperfectly purified, so that they may enter the joy of heaven (CCC 1030–1031). Our prayers help them because we are one body in Christ.
Why is 2 Maccabees missing from some Bibles?

It belongs to the deuterocanonical books, which were read in the Greek Old Testament used by the first Christians. The Catholic and Orthodox Churches receive them as Scripture. Many Protestant Bibles leave them out or print them separately. We can respect our fellow Christians while holding firmly to the canon the Church has received.
rite: The East Syriac tradition remembers the departed in every Holy Qurbana, and gives them a special day, the Friday of the Departed, before Great Lent. Today, in the season of the Dedication of the Church, Syro-Malabar families visit the cemeteries, clean and light the graves, and pray the Oppees for their dead. The readings explain these customs. We light the grave because Christ is the light of the dead; we pray because, like Judas, we believe in the resurrection; and we offer the Holy Qurbana because it is the one sacrifice that joins the living and the dead in Christ.
study: Ezekiel's answer, "O Lord God, you know", stands between yes and no. Where in my life do I need to say this to God?
2 Maccabees 12:44 says that praying for the dead makes sense only if they will rise. How does my prayer for my own dead show my faith in the resurrection?
1 Corinthians 15:58 ends with work, not with a dream. What "work of the Lord" can I do because I believe that my labour is not in vain?
Martha brings both her sorrow and her faith to Jesus (John 11:21–27). How can I help a grieving family to do the same?

lead: Both readings are about going home. Paul speaks of the "earthly tent" of our body and the "house not made with hands" that God has prepared for us. In the Gospel a lost son comes to himself and walks back to his father's house. In the season of the Dedication of the Church, the house of God is where the Father waits for every child.

r.h: A house not made with hands
set: In 2 Corinthians Paul defends his ministry, which is full of suffering. Just before this passage he says that "our outer nature is wasting away" while "our inner nature is being renewed day by day" (4:16). Paul was a tentmaker by trade (Acts 18:3), and he uses the image he knew best.
str: v. 1: the earthly tent and the eternal building from God.
vv. 2–4: we groan in this tent, longing to be "further clothed".
v. 5: God has prepared us and given the Spirit as a guarantee.
kw: A tent is light, temporary and easily taken down. So is our mortal body. But a tent is also where God once dwelt among his people.
A business word for a deposit paid in advance, which promises that the full price will follow. The Holy Spirit in us now is the first part of the glory to come (see also Ephesians 1:14).
vv: For we know that if the earthly tent we live in is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
Paul does not say "we hope" but "we know". Christian hope rests on what God has already done in raising Christ (4:14).
so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life
Paul does not long to escape from the body ("not to be unclothed") but to have it transformed ("to be further clothed"). The same picture of being swallowed up appears in 1 Corinthians 15:54.
He who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who has given us the Spirit as a guarantee.
Our future glory is not a vague wish. God himself has prepared us for it, and has already given a pledge.
ch: The Church prays in the same spirit at funerals. A preface of the Roman liturgy for the dead says that for the faithful "life is changed, not ended", and that when this earthly dwelling turns to dust, an eternal dwelling is made ready in heaven. The Catechism speaks of death as the end of our earthly pilgrimage and of our going home to God (CCC 1005, 1013).

r.h: He came to himself
set: Luke 15 contains three parables of the lost: the lost sheep, the lost coin and the lost son. Jesus tells them because the Pharisees and scribes were grumbling, "This fellow welcomes sinners and eats with them" (15:2). Today's reading gives the first half of the third parable; the elder brother comes in vv. 25–32.

For a son to ask for his inheritance while his father was alive was a deep insult, as if he wished his father dead. Pigs were unclean animals for Jews (Leviticus 11:7). To feed pigs for a Gentile was the lowest point a young Jew could reach.
str: vv. 11–12: the younger son asks for his share.
vv. 13–16: he wastes it and falls into hunger.
vv. 17–19: "he came to himself" and plans his confession.
v. 20: the father sees, has compassion, runs and embraces him.
vv. 21–24: the confession, and the father's feast.
kw: Conversion begins when a person sees the truth about himself. Sin is a kind of madness; repentance is coming back to one's senses.
From splanchna, the inner organs, the place of deep feeling. Luke uses the same verb for Jesus at the funeral of the widow's son (7:13) and for the Good Samaritan (10:33).
vv: But when he came to himself he said, ‘How many of my father’s hired hands have bread enough and to spare, but here I am dying of hunger!
His first motive is hunger, not love. The parable is honest: our conversion often begins with imperfect reasons, and the Father still receives us.
But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion; he ran and put his arms around him and kissed him.
The father must have been watching the road. In that culture an older man of standing did not run. The father lays aside his dignity, and runs before the son can finish his speech.
for this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found!
The robe, the ring and the sandals (v. 22) give back the place of a son; servants went barefoot. "Dead" and "alive again" are the language of resurrection.
ch: The Catechism describes the whole path of conversion through this parable: the son's fascination with an illusory freedom, his misery, his reflection, his confession, and the father's generous welcome (CCC 1439). St Jerome, in a letter to Pope Damasus on this parable, sees in the fatted calf Christ himself, offered for us and received in the Eucharist (in substance).

qa: Is the father in the parable too soft on sin?
No. The son's sin is not denied; he confesses it. But the parable shows that God's mercy goes ahead of us. The son is still "far off" when the father runs to him.
study: Paul calls the Holy Spirit a "guarantee" (2 Corinthians 5:5). What signs of this first instalment of glory can I see in my life now?
The younger son "came to himself" (Luke 15:17). What helps me to see the truth about myself and to return to the Father in the sacrament of Reconciliation?

lead: Both readings are about shepherds. In the Gospel the risen Jesus asks Peter three times, "Do you love me?", and gives him his flock to feed. In the Epistle, Peter, now an elder himself, passes the same charge on to the elders of the Church. The house of God is cared for by shepherds who love the chief Shepherd.

r.h: The chief shepherd will appear
set: 1 Peter is written to Christians scattered in Asia Minor (1:1), who suffer insults and hostility for their faith. The letter presents itself as written by Peter from "Babylon" (5:13), an early Christian name for Rome. Near its end the letter turns to the leaders of the communities.
str: v. 1: Peter speaks as a fellow elder and a witness of Christ's sufferings.
v. 2: tend the flock of God willingly and eagerly.
v. 3: not as lords, but as examples.
v. 4: the reward: the unfading crown of glory.
kw: Peter, the first of the apostles, does not command from above. He stands beside the elders as one of them. Presbyteros is the word from which "priest" comes.
Christ alone is the chief Shepherd. Every pastor in the Church is a shepherd under him and will give account to him.
From the amaranth, a flower that was said never to wither. Athletes won crowns of leaves that faded in days; the crown of glory never fades.
vv: as an elder myself and a witness of the sufferings of Christ
Peter's authority rests on what he saw. He watched the Lord suffer, and he himself had denied him. A shepherd who knows his own weakness can be gentle with the flock.
Do not lord it over those in your charge, but be examples to the flock.
The echo of the Gospel is clear: "the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them … It will not be so among you" (Matthew 20:25–26). The pastor leads by walking ahead, not by driving from behind.
And when the chief shepherd appears, you will win the crown of glory that never fades away.
The reward of a pastor is not money or honour now ("not for sordid gain", v. 2), but glory when Christ appears.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that bishops, with the priests as their co-workers, govern the Church as shepherds after the example of the Good Shepherd, who came not to be served but to serve (Lumen Gentium 27–28). St Gregory the Great, in his Pastoral Rule, insists that the one who leads must first be humble and must teach more by his life than by his words (in substance).

r.h: Feed my sheep
set: John 21 is an epilogue to the Gospel. By the Sea of Tiberias the risen Jesus gives the disciples a great catch of fish and a breakfast of bread and fish on a charcoal fire (21:9). The only other charcoal fire in the Gospels is in the courtyard of the high priest, where Peter denied Jesus three times (18:18).
str: v. 15: first question: "do you love me more than these?" "Feed my lambs."
v. 16: second question. "Tend my sheep."
v. 17: third question; Peter is hurt. "Feed my sheep."
vv. 18–19: Peter's death foretold, and the call: "Follow me."
kw: In vv. 15–16 Jesus asks with agapas, and Peter answers with philō; the third time Jesus too uses phileis. Some Fathers and teachers see a lesson in this change; many scholars think John uses the two verbs as synonyms. Either way, the threefold question matches the threefold denial.
The first means to give pasture, to feed; the second to shepherd, to guide and protect. Peter's office includes both: to nourish the flock with the word and sacraments, and to govern it.
vv: Simon son of John, do you love me more than these?
Jesus uses Peter's old name, as at his first call (1:42). "More than these" may mean more than the other disciples, recalling Peter's boast that he would never fall away (Matthew 26:33).
Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.
Peter no longer trusts his own strength. He appeals to the Lord's knowledge. This is humble love, which the Lord can build on.
when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and someone else will fasten a belt around you and take you where you do not wish to go.

John explains that this pointed to Peter's death (v. 19). St Clement of Rome already speaks of Peter's martyrdom, and later writers such as Tertullian and Eusebius record that he died in Rome under Nero, by crucifixion.
ch: St Augustine says that the threefold confession of love answered the threefold denial, so that love might speak as often as fear had spoken (in substance). The Catechism teaches that Jesus entrusted a specific authority to Peter, and that after the Resurrection he confirmed it with the words "Feed my sheep" (CCC 553; see also CCC 881).

study: Peter's authority comes from a love that has been forgiven (John 21:15–17). How does the memory of my own failures make me more gentle with others?
1 Peter 5:3 asks leaders to be "examples to the flock". Where am I a shepherd (in my family, my parish, my work), and what example do I give?

lead: Both readings open the doors of God's house to the nations. Paul announces the "mystery" that the Gentiles are fellow heirs with Israel. In the Gospel a Roman centurion shows a faith that amazes Jesus, and Jesus foresees many coming "from east and west" to the banquet of the kingdom. Today the Church also remembers Sts Zechariah and Elizabeth, the parents of John the Baptist.

r.h: Fellow heirs of the promise
set: Ephesians 2 has just described how Christ broke down "the dividing wall" between Jews and Gentiles and made them one new people (2:14–16), "a holy temple in the Lord" (2:21). In chapter 3 Paul, writing as a prisoner, explains his own part in this plan.
str: v. 1: Paul, a prisoner for the sake of the Gentiles.
vv. 2–4: the grace given to him, and the mystery made known by revelation.
v. 5: hidden in former generations, now revealed by the Spirit.
v. 6: the content of the mystery: the Gentiles are fellow heirs.
kw: Literally "the management of a household". God runs his house according to a plan, and Paul is given a steward's task in it (v. 2).
Not a secret kept from people but God's plan, once hidden and now opened. Here its content is precise: Jews and Gentiles together in one body.
fellow heirs, members of the same body, sharers
Paul makes three words beginning with "syn-", "together with". The Gentiles do not receive a second-class place; they share the same inheritance, the same body, the same promise.
vv: I Paul am a prisoner for Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles
Paul's chains are part of his mission. He was arrested in Jerusalem because he brought the gospel to the Gentiles (Acts 21:28; 22:21–22).
In former generations this mystery was not made known to humankind
The prophets had glimpsed that the nations would come to Zion (Isaiah 2:2–3), but the full form of the plan, one body in Christ, was revealed only after Easter.
that is, the Gentiles have become fellow heirs, members of the same body, and sharers in the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel.
The Gentiles are joined to the promise first made to Abraham. The Church does not replace Israel's hope; she is grafted into it (compare Romans 11:17–18).
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church is the new People of God, gathered from Jews and Gentiles and made one in the Spirit (Lumen Gentium 9). The same Council asks Christians to remember that the Church received the revelation of the Old Testament through the people of Israel (Nostra Aetate 4).

r.h: Only speak the word
set: After the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5–7), Matthew presents ten mighty works of Jesus (chapters 8–9). The first three heal people on the edge of Israel's community: a leper, the servant of a Gentile officer, and a woman, Peter's mother-in-law. Capernaum, on the Sea of Galilee, was Jesus' base during his ministry.

A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers. In Galilee he was probably in the service of Herod Antipas. Luke's account of the same event says that this man loved the Jewish people and built their synagogue (Luke 7:5).
str: vv. 5–6: the centurion's request.
v. 7: Jesus offers to come.
vv. 8–9: "I am not worthy"; the soldier's understanding of authority.
vv. 10–12: Jesus' amazement, and the saying about east and west.
v. 13: "let it be done for you according to your faith."
kw: An officer over about a hundred men. He knows what authority is: a word given, and it is done.
The Greek word can mean a child or a servant. Matthew's word is warm: this master cares deeply about one of his household.
vv: Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof; but only speak the word, and my servant will be healed.
A Jew who entered a Gentile house could become ritually unclean. The centurion spares Jesus this, and he believes that Jesus' word works at a distance, as God's word does.
Truly I tell you, in no one in Israel have I found such faith.
Only twice in the Gospels is Jesus said to be amazed: at this man's faith and at the unbelief of his own town (Mark 6:6).
many will come from east and west and will eat with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven

An echo of the prophets who saw the nations gathered for God's banquet (Isaiah 25:6). The warning of v. 12 about "the heirs of the kingdom" is not a judgment on the Jewish people as such; it warns everyone, Christians included, that belonging is not enough without faith.
ch: St Augustine says that by calling himself unworthy, the centurion became worthy to receive Christ, not under his roof but into his heart (in substance). The Roman liturgy places his words on the lips of every communicant before Holy Communion, and the Catechism quotes them in its teaching on the Eucharist (CCC 1386).

rite: Sts Zechariah and Elizabeth, remembered today, were "righteous before God" (Luke 1:6). Elizabeth was the first to greet Mary as "the mother of my Lord" (Luke 1:43). Like the centurion, they lived by trust in God's word, and Zechariah learned in silence to believe what the angel promised.
study: Ephesians 3:6 uses three "together" words. Who in my parish or neighbourhood feels like an outsider, and how can I help them share fully in the life of the Church?
The centurion believes that Jesus' word is enough (Matthew 8:8). Where do I need to trust the Lord's word without seeing the result at once?

lead: Both readings look at life in the household and at the reward that comes from the Lord. Paul teaches children, parents, slaves and masters to live every relationship "in the Lord". In the Gospel, Jesus tells of two sons: the one who said no but then went, and the one who said yes but did not go. What counts in God's house is not the first word but the will of the Father, done.

r.h: Doing the will of God from the heart
set: This passage belongs to the "household code" of Ephesians (5:21–6:9), which begins with the words "Be subject to one another out of reverence for Christ" (5:21). Such lists of duties were common in the Greek and Roman world. What is new is that every relationship is placed under Christ, and that the stronger party (parents, masters) also receives duties.
str: vv. 1–3: children and the commandment to honour parents.
v. 4: fathers: do not provoke your children.
vv. 5–8: slaves: serve as to the Lord.
v. 9: masters: the same Master in heaven, without partiality.
kw: The key phrase of the passage. Obedience and authority are not only social duties; they are lived inside the relationship with Christ.
Paul limits the father's power, which in Roman law was almost absolute. Harshness that crushes a child is against the Lord's way.
Literally "receiving the face": judging by appearance or rank. God does not do this (also Romans 2:11). Before him master and slave are equal.
vv: Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right.
Paul speaks directly to children, which means that they were present when the letter was read in the assembly. Children are full members of the Church.
And, fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.
Christian parents are the first teachers of the faith. The Lord's "discipline and instruction" is both correction and teaching, given with patience.
for you know that both of you have the same Master in heaven, and with him there is no partiality.

Paul does not attack slavery as an institution, which no one in his world could abolish, but he places within it a truth that would one day undo it: slave and master are brothers under one Lord (see Philemon 16).
ch: The Catechism treats the duties of children and parents under the fourth commandment (CCC 2197–2200, 2221–2223), and calls parents the first educators of their children. The Church today teaches clearly that slavery is gravely contrary to human dignity (Gaudium et Spes 27; CCC 2414). The lasting lesson of these verses is Paul's principle: every work done well, by anyone, is done for the Lord and will be rewarded by him (v. 8).

r.h: The son who changed his mind
set: Jesus has entered Jerusalem and cleansed the Temple. The chief priests and the elders of the people ask him by what authority he acts (21:23). He answers with a question about John the Baptist, and then with three parables: the two sons, the wicked tenants and the wedding banquet (21:28–22:14). The parable is addressed to these leaders, not to the Jewish people as a whole.
str: vv. 28–30: the father's request and the two answers.
v. 31a: "Which of the two did the will of his father?"
vv. 31b–32: the application: tax collectors and prostitutes believed John.
kw: The verb means to regret and change one's course. The same verb returns in v. 32: the leaders "did not change your minds". The parable is about this change.
John the Baptist came living and preaching the righteousness God asks for. Those who were thought far from God accepted his call; the religious experts did not.
vv: He answered, ‘I will not’; but later he changed his mind and went.

A note on the text. Some ancient manuscripts, among them Codex Vaticanus, tell the story in the opposite order: the first son says yes and does not go, the second says no and then goes, and the answer is "the second". The Malayalam POC follows that order. The meaning is the same in both forms.
Truly I tell you, the tax collectors and the prostitutes are going into the kingdom of God ahead of you.
"Ahead of you" leaves the door open. Jesus does not say that the leaders are shut out; he invites them to follow those who repented.
and even after you saw it, you did not change your minds and believe him.
The leaders saw sinners changed by John's preaching, and still did not change. The greatest obstacle to conversion is the belief that one does not need it.
ch: The parable explains another saying of Jesus: "Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only the one who does the will of my Father in heaven" (Matthew 7:21). It speaks to every believer whose words run ahead of his deeds. The Catechism teaches that conversion is a movement of a "contrite heart", drawn and moved by grace to respond to the merciful love of God (CCC 1428).

rite: On the First Friday many Syro-Malabar parishes keep the devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus, with confession, the Holy Qurbana and adoration. Today's Gospel fits it well: the Heart of Jesus is the heart of the Father who waits for the son who said no, and welcomes him when he changes his mind and goes.
study: Ephesians 6 places every relationship "in the Lord". Which of my relationships at home or at work most needs to be lived in this way?
Am I more like the son who says yes and does not go, or the one who says no and then goes (Matthew 21:28–30)? What would it mean for me to "change my mind" today?

lead: Both readings describe love that is real. Paul gives a string of short commands: "Let love be genuine", bless your persecutors, weep with those who weep. In the Gospel a lawyer asks, "who is my neighbor?", and Jesus answers with the Samaritan who stopped on the road. In God's house love is not a feeling only; it is the way to eternal life.

r.h: Let love be genuine
set: In Romans 1–11 Paul has explained the gospel: all have sinned, and all are justified by grace through faith in Christ. Chapter 12 turns to life. It begins: "present your bodies as a living sacrifice" (12:1), and describes the Church as one body with many members (12:4–8). Today's verses show what that body looks like in daily life.
str: vv. 9–13: love within the community: genuine, warm, zealous, hopeful, generous, hospitable.
vv. 14–16: love toward everyone: blessing persecutors, sharing joy and sorrow, humility.
vv. 17–18: love in conflict: no revenge, peace with all as far as possible.
kw: Literally "love without hypocrisy". A hypokritēs was an actor wearing a mask. Christian love is not a performance.
Paul uses words from family life. In the Church we love one another as brothers and sisters, with the warm affection of a family.
Literally "love of strangers". Paul says "pursue" it (v. 13): do not only wait for guests, but go after the chance to welcome.
vv: Let love be genuine; hate what is evil, hold fast to what is good;
Genuine love is not weak. It hates evil and holds on to good, like someone holding something precious with both hands.
Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep.
The second is often easier than the first. To rejoice sincerely in another's success, without envy, is a sign of real love.
Do not repay anyone evil for evil

Paul echoes Jesus' teaching in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:39, 44). Peace with all is asked "so far as it depends on you" (v. 18): we cannot control others, but we can refuse to answer evil with evil.
ch: The Catechism quotes St Paul's praise of love and teaches that charity animates and inspires the practice of all the virtues (CCC 1826–1827). St Augustine's short rule, "Love, and do what you will", means that when the root of a life is genuine love, good actions grow from it (in substance; Homilies on 1 John 7).

r.h: Who is my neighbour?
set: Jesus is on his long journey to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51–19:27). A lawyer, an expert in the law of Moses, asks a test question. Jesus lets him answer from the Scriptures: Deuteronomy 6:5 (love of God) and Leviticus 19:18 (love of neighbour).

The road from Jerusalem down to Jericho drops about a thousand metres in some twenty-seven kilometres, through lonely desert hills where robbers could hide.
