Jews and Samaritans were divided by long hostility over the Temple and the Scriptures (see John 4:9). A Samaritan is the last hero Jesus' hearers would expect.
str: vv. 25–28: the question about eternal life and the two commandments.
v. 29: "And who is my neighbor?"
vv. 30–32: the man left half dead; the priest and the Levite pass by.
vv. 33–35: the Samaritan's compassion and care.
vv. 36–37: Jesus' question and command: "Go and do likewise."
kw: Literally "the one nearby". The lawyer wants to know where the circle of duty ends. Jesus changes the question: not "who is my neighbour?" but "who acted as a neighbour?"
The same verb as the father of the prodigal son (15:20) and Jesus himself (7:13). The Samaritan feels in his inner self what God feels.
About a day's wage for a labourer (Matthew 20:2). Two denarii could pay for several days at the inn, and the Samaritan promises more.
vv: And who is my neighbor?
The lawyer asks "wanting to justify himself". He wants a limit. Love that looks for limits is not yet the love the law commands.
But a Samaritan while traveling came near him; and when he saw him, he was moved with pity.

The priest and the Levite "saw" and passed by; the Samaritan "saw" and came near. They may have feared ritual impurity from touching a body that seemed dead (Leviticus 21:1), but the parable gives them no excuse. The Samaritan takes the risk and pays the cost.
Go and do likewise.
The lawyer cannot bring himself to say "the Samaritan"; he says "the one who showed him mercy". Jesus sends him out to become that kind of person.
ch: Many Fathers, among them Origen, St Ambrose and St Augustine, read the parable also as a picture of salvation: the wounded man is Adam, fallen on the way from paradise; the Samaritan is Christ, who comes near to us; the oil and wine are the sacraments; the inn is the Church; and the promise to return is Christ's second coming (in substance). Pope Francis devotes the second chapter of the encyclical Fratelli Tutti to this parable, asking each of us which character we are.

study: Romans 12:15 asks me to rejoice with those who rejoice. Whose success do I find it hard to celebrate, and why?
Jesus turns the question "Who is my neighbour?" into "Who acted as a neighbour?" (Luke 10:29, 36). Whom have I passed by on the other side, and how can I come near?

lead: On the second Sunday of Qudash Edtha the readings speak of an inheritance. In Exodus, God promises slaves in Egypt a land “for a possession”. In Isaiah, the Servant who seems to have labored in vain knows that his reward is with God. Peter tells scattered Christians that they have been born anew into an inheritance kept in heaven. In Matthew, Jesus promises those who leave everything for his name a hundredfold and eternal life. The season looks at the Church as God's house; today's readings show what that house is for: a people God has made his own, on the way to an inheritance that cannot fade.

The key words are promise, possession and reward. Each reading also has a time of testing before the gift: brick-making in Egypt, hidden years in a quiver, “various trials”, and the hard saying about riches.

r.h: “I am the Lord”: the promises of deliverance
set: Moses has gone to Pharaoh for the first time, and things have got worse. Pharaoh orders the Israelites to make bricks without being given straw, and the Israelite foremen blame Moses (Exodus 5). Moses turns to God with a bitter question: “Why did you ever send me?” (5:22). Chapter 6 is God's answer. It does not begin with an explanation but with God's name and a chain of promises.

Many scholars see 6:2–8 as a second account of Moses' call, parallel to the burning bush in chapter 3, from another strand of Israel's tradition. Placed here, after failure, it carries a message: God's plan is not defeated by the first setback.
str: v. 1: “Now you shall see”: God's answer to Moses' complaint.
vv. 2–3: “I am the Lord”: the name, and the God of the patriarchs.
vv. 4–5: the covenant with the fathers; God hears the groaning of the slaves.
vv. 6–8: the message for Israel: a chain of “I will” promises, closed again by “I am the Lord”.
¶ The passage is framed by the same words, “I am the Lord” (vv. 2 and 8, and again in v. 6). Everything promised in between rests on who God is.
kw: The sacred name revealed to Moses at the bush (3:14–15). Out of reverence Jews do not pronounce it; they say Adonai, “the Lord”, and the Greek and Latin Bibles and our own translations do the same. It is the name of a God who is present and faithful.
The name by which God was known to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Genesis 17:1; 35:11). Its original meaning is uncertain; the ancient translations rendered it “Almighty”.
The verb behind the gō’ēl, the next of kin who buys back a relative sold into slavery or recovers his land (Leviticus 25:25, 47–49). God acts as Israel's next of kin: these slaves are his family.
Something received to hold as a heritage. The land is a gift, not a prize won by Israel's own strength.
vv: I have also heard the groaning of the Israelites whom the Egyptians are holding as slaves, and I have remembered my covenant.
In the Bible, for God to “remember” is not to recall something forgotten; it is to act on a promise. The groaning of the slaves and the promise to the fathers meet in God's memory.
I will free you from the burdens of the Egyptians and deliver you from slavery to them. I will redeem you with an outstretched arm
The “outstretched arm” is the image of God's power at work in the Exodus (Deuteronomy 4:34; 26:8).
I will take you as my people, and I will be your God.

This is the heart of the covenant, a formula repeated through the prophets (Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:28) and at the very end of the Bible (Revelation 21:3). The land is given so that a people may belong to God. Jewish tradition links the four verbs of vv. 6–7 (bring out, deliver, redeem, take) with the four cups of wine at the Passover meal.
I will bring you into the land that I swore to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; I will give it to you for a possession.
ch: The Catechism says that the revelation of the divine name to Moses proved to be the fundamental one for both the Old and the New Covenants, and that the name expresses God's faithfulness in spite of human sin (CCC 204, 211). The memory of the Exodus is the pattern of the Christian memorial: when the Church remembers God's saving deeds in the liturgy, they become present (CCC 1363). The New Testament says that Christ “redeemed” us (Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 1:18–19): in the Incarnation God became our next of kin in the flesh.

r.h: A light to the nations
set: This is the second of the four Servant Songs in the Book of Consolation (Isaiah 42:1–9; 49:1–6; 50:4–9; 52:13–53:12). The setting is the end of the Babylonian exile. Here the Servant himself speaks, to the coastlands and the peoples far away.

Who is the Servant? In v. 3 he is called “Israel”, yet in v. 5 his mission is to bring Israel back to God. He is Israel as God meant it to be: one who carries the people's vocation and serves the people. The New Testament sees this figure fulfilled in Jesus.
str: vv. 1–3: the call from the womb; the hidden weapon; “You are my servant, Israel”.
v. 4: the Servant's discouragement, and his trust.
vv. 5–6: the mission widened: not only the tribes of Jacob but the end of the earth.
v. 7: the despised one before whom kings will stand up.
kw: A word of honour as well as of service: Moses and David are each called the Lord's servant. The Servant belongs wholly to God.
The pay a worker receives at the end of the day (v. 4). The Servant leaves the account of his labour with God.
God's salvation is not for Israel alone. Simeon sings these words over the child Jesus (Luke 2:32), and Paul and Barnabas take them as their own command (Acts 13:47).
vv: The Lord called me before I was born, while I was in my mother’s womb he named me.
Jeremiah heard the same call (Jeremiah 1:5), and Paul uses this language of his own vocation (Galatians 1:15). A vocation begins in God's choice, before any merit.
he made me a polished arrow, in his quiver he hid me away.
A sharpened arrow is kept in the quiver until the moment it is needed. Hidden years are not wasted years.
I have labored in vain, I have spent my strength for nothing and vanity; yet surely my cause is with the Lord, and my reward with my God.
The honest cry of every apostle who sees little fruit. The answer is not success but trust: the outcome belongs to God.
I will give you as a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth.
ch: The Catechism says that the characteristics of the Messiah are revealed above all in the Servant Songs, which proclaim the meaning of Jesus' Passion (CCC 713). The Second Vatican Council opened its constitution on the Church with the words “Christ is the light of nations”, a light that shines on the face of the Church (Lumen Gentium 1). On a Sunday of Qudash Edtha this is the Church's mission: to carry that light to the end of the earth.

r.h: An inheritance kept in heaven
set: 1 Peter is addressed to “the exiles of the Dispersion” in five provinces of Asia Minor (1:1). Most of them were converts from paganism, living as a small minority and suffering suspicion and slander for their faith. The letter is sent from “Babylon” (5:13), a code name for Rome.

Today's passage is the opening blessing. It follows the Jewish form of prayer that begins “Blessed be God” (the berakah). Many scholars hear in the letter the echo of teaching given at baptism: new birth, hope, testing and joy.
str: v. 3: blessing of the Father, who has given us new birth into a living hope.
v. 4: the inheritance and its three qualities.
v. 5: God's power guards us until the salvation to be revealed.
vv. 6–7: joy in trials; faith tested like gold.
kw: To beget again. The same idea as being born “from above” (John 3:3–5) and the “water of rebirth” (Titus 3:5). The Christian life begins with a birth that God gives.
The Greek Old Testament uses this word for the land promised to Israel. Peter now uses it for the gift kept in heaven.

Three words that each begin with the Greek “not”. The last gave its name to the amaranth, the flower thought never to fade. The promised land could be ravaged, defiled or lost; this inheritance cannot.
A military word: a garrison guarding a town. While the inheritance is kept in heaven, the heirs are guarded on earth.
vv: By his great mercy he has given us a new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,
Hope is “living” because its foundation is a living person, the risen Christ.
and into an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you,
more precious than gold that, though perishable, is tested by fire
Gold was refined in the furnace to remove its impurities. Trials do not destroy faith; they show that it is real. Notice the link with today's Gospel: gold perishes, faith remains.
ch: The Catechism teaches that through baptism we are delivered from sin and reborn as children of God (CCC 1213), and that hope responds to the desire for happiness that God has placed in every heart (CCC 1818). Because of its many baptismal themes, 1 Peter is read on the Sundays of Easter in one year of the Roman lectionary, the season when the Church welcomes the newly baptized. What we receive at the font is not a reward for this life but the pledge of the life to come.

r.h: Who then can be saved?
set: The passage follows directly on the rich young man (19:16–22), who asked what good deed would bring eternal life and went away grieving, for he had many possessions. Jesus now speaks to his disciples about what they have just seen.

Many people of the time took wealth as a sign of God's blessing (compare Job 42:10–12; Deuteronomy 28:1–14). That is why the disciples are astonished: if the blessed rich cannot easily enter, who can?
str: vv. 23–24: the hard saying: the camel and the needle.
vv. 25–26: “Who can be saved?” “For God all things are possible.”
v. 27: Peter's question: “What then will we have?”
vv. 28–29: a double promise: thrones for the Twelve; a hundredfold and eternal life for all who leave things for his name.
v. 30: the great reversal.
kw: The largest animal in Palestine passing through the smallest opening: a deliberate picture of the impossible, in Jesus' typical style of exaggeration (compare the log in the eye, 7:3–5).
Literally “new birth” or “regeneration”. In the New Testament the word appears only here and in Titus 3:5. It speaks of the world made new at the end, the same hope as Peter's “new birth”.
An overflowing return. Mark's version adds “with persecutions” (Mark 10:30): the reward includes the cross.
vv: it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for someone who is rich to enter the kingdom of God.
Matthew, who usually says “kingdom of heaven”, here writes “kingdom of God”. The two mean the same: “heaven” is a reverent way of saying “God”.
For mortals it is impossible, but for God all things are possible.
An echo of the angel's word to Mary (Luke 1:37) and of God's word to Abraham (Genesis 18:14). Salvation is always God's gift; a rich man too can be saved by grace, as Zacchaeus was (Luke 19:1–10).
you who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
The Twelve are the foundation of the renewed people of God. “Judging” here also carries the Old Testament sense of ruling and leading, as the judges of Israel did.
And everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or children or fields, for my name’s sake, will receive a hundredfold, and will inherit eternal life.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus asks his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone, and that detachment from riches is necessary for entering the Kingdom (CCC 2544, 2556). It sees in the Twelve, with Peter at their head, the structure the Lord gave to his community: representing the twelve tribes of Israel, they are the foundation stones of the new Jerusalem (CCC 765). Clement of Alexandria, in his homily “Who is the rich man that shall be saved?”, teaches that the Lord does not condemn possessions themselves but the soul's attachment to them; riches are to be used for others (in substance).

qa: Was there a gate in Jerusalem called “the Eye of the Needle”?

This explanation is popular, but there is no ancient evidence for such a gate; it appears only in much later writers. A few late manuscripts read kamilos, “rope”, instead of kamēlos, “camel”, probably to soften the saying. Jesus means the impossible, and then says that God does the impossible (19:26).
If God is called “the Lord” in Genesis, why does Exodus 6:3 say the patriarchs did not know this name?

Genesis does use the name, even in God's own words to the patriarchs (Genesis 15:7; 28:13). Exodus 6:3 means that they had not yet known the full meaning of the name. That meaning is shown in the Exodus: the Lord is the God who delivers and redeems. Scholars also note that these books join different strands of tradition.
Must every Christian leave home and family?

Some are called to leave everything literally, as priests and religious do. All are called to put Christ first and to hold everything for his name's sake (CCC 2544–2545). The Gospel does not abandon families; in the family of the Church they are received back “a hundredfold”.
rite: Qudash Edtha is the last season of the East Syriac liturgical year; its Sundays look at the Church as God's dwelling and as the bride on her way to the Kingdom. Today's Gospel promises thrones to the Twelve. For the St Thomas Christians this has a family meaning: our Church traces its faith to one of those Twelve, the apostle Thomas, who left everything and, as our tradition holds, came to India. In the Holy Qurbana we already receive the pledge of the inheritance Peter speaks of, kept in heaven and given to us at the altar.
study: Exodus 6 begins after failure and complaint. When my efforts for God seem to make things worse, which of the “I will” promises do I most need to hear?
Isaiah's Servant says, “I have labored in vain”, yet leaves his reward with God. Where do I need to leave the results with God?
Peter calls our inheritance “imperishable, undefiled, and unfading”. What perishable things compete with it in my heart?
What has my family received “a hundredfold” through faith, and what might Jesus be asking me to leave for his name?

lead: Two confessions of who Christ is. Paul's hymn in Colossians sings of Christ as the image of the invisible God and the head of the body, the Church. At Caesarea Philippi Peter confesses Jesus as the Messiah, the Son of the living God, and Jesus promises to build his Church on that rock. In the season of the Church's dedication, the readings show the Church's head and her foundation.

r.h: The image of the invisible God
set: Colossae was a small town in the Lycus valley of Asia Minor, near Laodicea. Paul had not founded the church there himself; Epaphras had (1:7). Some teachers were offering extra ways to God through angelic “powers”, special feasts and visions (2:16–18). Paul answers with a hymn that sets Christ above every power in heaven and on earth.
str: vv. 12–14: thanksgiving: rescued from darkness, brought into the kingdom of the Son.
vv. 15–17: Christ and creation: all things through him and for him.
vv. 18–20: Christ and the new creation: head of the Church, firstborn from the dead, peace through the blood of his cross.
kw: In Genesis man is made “in the image” of God (Genesis 1:27). Christ is the image itself: in him the invisible God becomes visible (compare John 14:9).
Not the first creature, but the one who has the rights and first place of the eldest son. The same word is used of his resurrection: “the firstborn from the dead” (v. 18).
The whole of God's being and life. It does not dwell partly in angels and partly in Christ; all of it dwells in him (compare 2:9).
vv: He has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son,
The Greek verb for “transferred” was also used for moving a whole population from one land to another. Baptism is such a transfer: a change of king.
He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation;
He is the head of the body, the church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he might come to have first place in everything.
Earlier letters call the Church the body of Christ (1 Corinthians 12:27). Colossians adds that Christ is its head: the source of its life and unity.
ch: The Catechism quotes this hymn to teach that God created all things through the eternal Word, his beloved Son (CCC 291), and that Christ is the head of his body, the Church (CCC 792). When the Arians argued that “firstborn of all creation” made the Son a creature, St Athanasius answered that he is called firstborn not because he was the first to be made, but because he came down to creatures and became the brother of many (in substance). The Council of Nicaea confessed him “begotten, not made”.

r.h: You are the Messiah
set: Caesarea Philippi lay at the foot of Mount Hermon, by the springs of the Jordan, some 40 km north of the Sea of Galilee. It was a pagan city: Herod the Great had built a temple there to the emperor Augustus, and there was a cave shrine of the god Pan (the place is still called Banias). Among rival gods and emperors, Jesus asks who he is.
str: vv. 13–14: what people say: John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah, one of the prophets.
vv. 15–16: “But who do you say that I am?” Peter's confession.
vv. 17–19: Jesus' answer: a blessing, a new name, the Church, the keys.
v. 20: the command to keep silent.
kw: A play on words. In Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke, both are kêphā, which is why Paul calls Peter “Cephas” (1 Corinthians 15:5; Galatians 2:9).
The assembly of those called together. The Greek Old Testament uses it for the assembly of Israel. In the Gospels the word occurs only twice, both times in Matthew (here and 18:17).
The image comes from Isaiah 22:22, where the master of the king's palace receives “the key of the house of David”. Keys mean authority to govern the household.
vv: But who do you say that I am?
The “you” is plural: the question is put to all the disciples, and Peter answers for them.
And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.
“The gates of Hades” are the power of death. Not even death will overcome the Church that Christ builds.
whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.
“Bind” and “loose” were rabbinic terms for forbidding and permitting, and for imposing and lifting a ban. Heaven ratifies the decisions of the one to whom the keys are given.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ built his Church on the rock of the faith confessed by Peter (CCC 424); that Peter holds a unique place among the Twelve; and that the “power of the keys” means authority to govern the house of God, which the risen Jesus confirmed with the words “Feed my sheep” (CCC 552–553). The Church sees this ministry continued in the Bishop of Rome, the successor of Peter, “the perpetual and visible principle and foundation of unity” of bishops and faithful (Lumen Gentium 23; CCC 882).

qa: Is the rock Peter, or Peter's faith?

Both readings are found in the Fathers, and they belong together. The play on words points to Peter himself, the man Jesus is speaking to; but Peter is the rock as the one who confesses the faith revealed by the Father. The Catechism holds both: Christ built his Church on the rock of the faith confessed by Peter (CCC 424), and he gave the keys to Peter himself (CCC 553).
study: Paul says that in Christ “all things hold together”. What in my life is falling apart, and how can I bring it to him?
If Jesus asked me today, “Who do you say that I am?”, what would my answer be, in one sentence?

lead: Peter, near the end of his life, remembers the mountain where he saw the glory of Christ and heard the Father's voice. Luke tells the same event: Jesus at prayer, transfigured, speaking with Moses and Elijah about his “departure” at Jerusalem. The Epistle is the witness; the Gospel is the scene. The Church's faith rests on apostles who saw and heard, and on Scriptures the Spirit inspired.

r.h: We had been eyewitnesses
set: 2 Peter is written as Peter's testament: a farewell letter in which a dying leader reminds his people of what matters (compare Paul's farewell in Acts 20 and 2 Timothy 4). Its readers were troubled by teachers who mocked the hope of Christ's coming (3:3–4). Many scholars think it was written after Peter's death by a disciple, in his name and tradition; the Church receives it as inspired Scripture and as the witness of Peter.
str: vv. 12–15: Peter's purpose: to remind them before his death.
vv. 16–18: not myths but eyewitness: the Transfiguration.
vv. 19–21: the prophetic word, a lamp in a dark place, given by the Holy Spirit.
kw: Peter calls his body a tent (vv. 13–14), soon to be folded away. The NRSV says “this body”; the Malayalam POC keeps the image of the tent.

A rare word, used in Greek religion for those who had reached the highest grade of initiation and had “seen” the mysteries. Peter's mystery is not a secret rite: he saw Christ's majesty with his own eyes.
Literally “light-bearer”, the morning star that announces the day: Christ rising in the heart (compare Revelation 22:16).
vv: For we did not follow cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we had been eyewitnesses of his majesty.
Peter sets myth against eyewitness: the Christian faith rests on what happened in history.
We ourselves heard this voice come from heaven, while we were with him on the holy mountain.
The mountain is “holy” because God revealed himself there, as on Sinai. Later tradition identified it with Mount Tabor.
no prophecy ever came by human will, but men and women moved by the Holy Spirit spoke from God.
“Moved” (pheromenoi) is the word used for a ship driven by the wind (Acts 27:15, 17). The human authors truly wrote, but the Spirit filled their sails.
ch: The Second Vatican Council cites this passage when it teaches that the books of Scripture were written under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit and have God as their author, while the human writers used their own powers as true authors (Dei Verbum 11; CCC 105–106). Verse 20 also gives a rule for reading: Scripture is to be read within the living Tradition of the whole Church, not by private interpretation alone (Dei Verbum 12; CCC 113).

r.h: This is my Son, my Chosen
set: About eight days earlier Peter had confessed Jesus as the Messiah of God, and Jesus had begun to speak of his suffering and of taking up the cross (9:18–27). The Transfiguration confirms both: Jesus is the Son in glory, and the way to glory goes through Jerusalem. Only Luke says that Jesus went up to pray and was transfigured while praying, and only Luke tells us what Moses and Elijah spoke about.
str: vv. 28–29: Jesus goes up to pray; his face and clothes change.
vv. 30–31: Moses and Elijah speak of his departure.
vv. 32–33: the sleepy disciples; Peter's three dwellings.
vv. 34–36: the cloud, the voice, and Jesus alone.
kw: Literally “exodus”, a going out. Jesus' death, resurrection and ascension are the new Exodus, to be “accomplished” at Jerusalem.
Booths like those of the Feast of Tabernacles. Peter wants to make the moment last; but the true tent of God's presence will be Christ's own glorified body.
The cloud overshadows them as the power of the Most High overshadowed Mary (Luke 1:35), and as the cloud covered the tent of meeting (Exodus 40:35, in the Greek Bible).
vv: And while he was praying, the appearance of his face changed, and his clothes became dazzling white.
Prayer is the place of transfiguration. Luke shows Jesus praying at every turning point: at his baptism, before choosing the Twelve, before Peter's confession (3:21; 6:12; 9:18).
They appeared in glory and were speaking of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.
Moses and Elijah stand for the Law and the Prophets, and both speak of the Cross.
Then from the cloud came a voice that said, “This is my Son, my Chosen; listen to him!”
“My Chosen” recalls the Servant of Isaiah 42:1; “listen to him” recalls Moses' promise of a prophet like himself (Deuteronomy 18:15).
ch: The Catechism sees in the Transfiguration a foretaste of Christ's glorious coming and a strengthening of the disciples before the Passion (CCC 554–556). It quotes St Thomas Aquinas: the whole Trinity appeared, the Father in the voice, the Son in the man, the Spirit in the shining cloud (CCC 555). The voice from the cloud gives the Church her daily task: to listen to the Son.

study: Peter writes so that his readers may “recall these things” after his death. Who handed on the faith to me, and how am I handing it on?
Jesus was transfigured while praying. What place does quiet prayer have in my day?

lead: Two wedding feasts. In Revelation, heaven sings Hallelujah because the marriage of the Lamb has come and his bride has made herself ready. In Matthew, a king's wedding banquet is refused by the invited guests and filled with people from the streets, but one guest has no wedding robe. The invitation is for all; the garment is what we must accept with it.

r.h: The marriage supper of the Lamb
set: Chapters 17–18 described the fall of “Babylon”, the great city that stands for every power drunk with luxury and with the blood of the saints; for John's first readers it was Rome. Chapter 19 opens in heaven with the answer of praise. After the fall of the false city, the bride appears.
str: vv. 1–4: three Hallelujahs over the judgment of Babylon; the elders and the living creatures worship.
v. 5: a voice from the throne calls all God's servants to praise.
vv. 6–8: the fourth Hallelujah: the Lord reigns; the marriage of the Lamb has come.
vv. 9–10: the beatitude of those invited; the angel refuses worship.
kw: Hebrew for “Praise the Lord” (hallĕlû yāh), familiar from the Psalms. In the New Testament it appears only in this chapter, four times.
The Church, ready for her husband. The prophets had called Israel the Lord's bride (Hosea 2; Isaiah 62:5).
Bright, pure linen; the text itself explains it as the righteous deeds of the saints. Notice that it “has been granted” to her: the garment is a gift, and also a life lived.
vv: for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his bride has made herself ready;
The bridegroom is the Lamb that was slain (5:6). The marriage is the full communion of Christ and his people at the end of time.
Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.
One of the seven beatitudes of Revelation. Every Eucharist is a foretaste of this supper.
You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you … Worship God!
Even the angel who reveals the mysteries refuses worship. Worship belongs to God alone.
ch: The Catechism calls the Eucharist the Lord's Supper, which anticipates the wedding feast of the Lamb in the heavenly Jerusalem (CCC 1329), and speaks of the Church as the bride of Christ (CCC 796). The whole story of salvation is a love story that ends in a wedding.

r.h: Come to the wedding banquet
set: This is the third of three parables Jesus tells in the Temple after his entry into Jerusalem (21:28–22:14), addressed to the chief priests and elders who had questioned his authority (21:23). Luke has a similar parable of a great dinner (Luke 14:15–24); Matthew's version adds the king, his son, the violent response, and the man without a wedding robe.
str: vv. 1–7: the first invitations refused; the servants mistreated; the king's anger.
vv. 8–10: the invitation goes out to the streets; the hall is filled with good and bad.
vv. 11–13: the guest without a wedding robe.
v. 14: “Many are called, but few are chosen.”
kw: The prophets picture the age of salvation as a feast (Isaiah 25:6). This feast is for the king's son: the Kingdom is the marriage of God's Son with humanity.
Some think the host provided festive garments; this is uncertain. What is clear is that the guest came in as he was and did not let the invitation change him.
In Semitic speech “many” can mean “all”. All are called; those who respond are chosen. The saying is a warning, not a head count.
vv: But they made light of it and went away, one to his farm, another to his business,
The refusals are not wicked in themselves: a farm, a business. The danger is ordinary things that seem more urgent than God's invitation.
Go therefore into the main streets, and invite everyone you find to the wedding banquet.
Friend, how did you get in here without a wedding robe?
He is called “friend” and given a chance to answer; but he is speechless.
ch: The Catechism cites this parable when it says that Jesus invites people to the feast of the Kingdom but also asks for a radical choice (CCC 546). St Gregory the Great, preaching on this Gospel, taught that the wedding garment is charity: one may enter the Church by faith, but without love one is not dressed for the feast (in substance). Verse 7 is often seen as reflecting the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70; its lesson is the seriousness of refusing God's invitation, not a judgment on the Jewish people (CCC 597).

qa: Is it unfair to throw out a man brought in from the street?

The parable describes the Kingdom, not a social event. The invitation is undeserved, but it is not without consequence. To accept it means to “put on” Christ (Galatians 3:27; Romans 13:14) and to let grace change one's life.
study: What “farm” or “business” most often makes me too busy for God's invitation?
Revelation says the bride's linen is “the righteous deeds of the saints”. What one deed of love can I weave into that garment today?

lead: Both readings speak the language of a wedding, and of the friend who brings the bride to the bridegroom. Paul has betrothed the Corinthians to Christ and fears that they will be led astray. John the Baptist rejoices to hear the bridegroom's voice and steps aside: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” Every minister of the Church is only the bridegroom's friend.

r.h: Betrothed to one husband
set: In chapters 10–13 Paul defends his ministry against rival preachers whom he calls, with irony, “super-apostles” (11:5). They were impressive speakers who boasted of their credentials and looked down on Paul. Paul asks the Corinthians to bear with his “foolishness”: he will boast, not to praise himself but to win them back.
str: v. 1: “Bear with me in a little foolishness.”
v. 2: Paul's divine jealousy: he has betrothed them to Christ.
v. 3: his fear: the serpent and Eve.
v. 4: another Jesus, another spirit, another gospel.
kw: Not envy, but God's passionate love for his people, which will not share them with idols (Exodus 20:5; Hosea 2).
to betroth, to join in marriage
Paul acts like the father or friend who arranges a marriage and presents the bride on the wedding day.
Undivided devotion: the opposite of a heart split between Christ and others.
vv: I feel a divine jealousy for you, for I promised you in marriage to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.
The betrothal took place when they believed and were baptized; the presentation will be at Christ's coming. The time between is the time of faithfulness.
But I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ.
The danger is not open hostility but clever deception, as in Eden.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the theme of Christ as Bridegroom of the Church was prepared by the prophets and announced by John the Baptist, and that the Apostle speaks of the whole Church and of each believer as a bride “betrothed” to Christ (CCC 796). It also calls virginity for the sake of the Kingdom a powerful sign of the supremacy of the bond with Christ and of the ardent awaiting of his return (CCC 1619).

r.h: The friend of the bridegroom
set: After the conversation with Nicodemus, Jesus and his disciples baptize in Judea, while John is still baptizing at Aenon near Salim. The exact place is uncertain; it was probably in the Jordan valley or in Samaria. John's disciples are troubled that “all are going to him”. John's answer is his last testimony in this Gospel. (John 4:2 adds that it was not Jesus himself but his disciples who baptized.)
str: vv. 22–24: two baptizing ministries side by side.
vv. 25–26: a discussion about purification; the complaint of John's disciples.
vv. 27–28: John: everything is a gift from heaven; “I am not the Messiah.”
vv. 29–30: the bridegroom, his friend, and joy fulfilled.
kw: In the prophets the Lord himself is Israel's bridegroom (Isaiah 62:5). To call Jesus the bridegroom is a quiet confession of who he is.
At Jewish weddings a close friend (later called the shoshbin) helped arrange the marriage and prepare the feast; he did not take the bride for himself.
The word of God's plan. “He must increase” is not resignation but John's glad acceptance of God's will.
vv: No one can receive anything except what has been given from heaven.
John sees his own mission, and Jesus' success, as gifts. There is no room for rivalry.
He who has the bride is the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice.
The friend's joy is to hear the bridegroom's voice, not his own. That is the joy of every true minister.
He must increase, but I must decrease.
ch: The Catechism presents John the Baptist as the one who announced Christ the Bridegroom (CCC 796) and as the Lord's immediate forerunner, sent to prepare his way (CCC 523). St Augustine observes that the Church celebrates John's birth in June, when the days begin to shorten, and Christ's birth in December, when the days begin to lengthen, as a sign of these words: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (in substance).

qa: Who is “a Jew” in verse 25?

Simply an unnamed Jewish man who debated with John's disciples about purification, perhaps comparing John's baptism with Jewish rites of washing or with Jesus' baptism. John and his disciples were Jews too; the verse does not set “the Jews” against the Gospel.
study: Paul fears that the Corinthians will be led away from “a sincere and pure devotion to Christ”. What divides my heart?
Where in my family, parish or work do I need to decrease, so that Christ may increase?

lead: Two voices speak of heaven. Paul, forced to defend himself, tells of being caught up into Paradise, yet refuses to boast except of his weaknesses. In John, the one who comes from above testifies to what he has seen and heard, and whoever believes in the Son has eternal life. We know heaven not by our own ascents but because the Son came down.

r.h: Caught up into Paradise
set: Paul is still answering the “super-apostles”, who boasted of visions and revelations. Reluctantly he matches them. He speaks of “a person in Christ” in the third person, but the context (12:7) shows that he means himself. Fourteen years before this letter, written around AD 55–57, would be the early 40s, before his great missionary journeys.
str: v. 1: boasting gains nothing, but he will go on to visions.
vv. 2–4: the man caught up to the third heaven, into Paradise.
v. 5: he will boast of that man, but of himself only in weakness.
¶ The passage leads straight into the “thorn in the flesh” and the Lord's answer: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (12:9).
kw: Jewish writings of the time spoke of several heavens, often three or seven. For Paul the third heaven is the highest: the presence of God.
A word of Persian origin meaning a walled garden or park. The Greek Old Testament uses it for the garden of Eden; here it is the place of God's presence (compare Luke 23:43).
things that are not to be told
Words that cannot or may not be spoken. Paul does not satisfy curiosity; the vision is not his message.
vv: I know a person in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven
“Caught up” (harpazō) is the verb used for being taken up to meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17). Paul did not climb; he was taken.
was caught up into Paradise and heard things that are not to be told, that no mortal is permitted to repeat.
On behalf of such a one I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except of my weaknesses.
The apostle's credentials are not his visions but his weakness, where Christ's power is seen.
ch: St Augustine took this passage as the starting point for his teaching on the kinds of vision: bodily sight, the seeing of images in the spirit, and the intellectual vision of the mind, which he thought Paul was granted in the third heaven (in substance; The Literal Meaning of Genesis, Book 12). The Church learns from Paul's restraint: the Catechism teaches that later private revelations do not complete Christ's definitive Revelation but help us to live by it (CCC 67). Paul himself puts the vision beneath the Cross: power made perfect in weakness.

r.h: The one who comes from above
set: It is not clear whether these verses continue the words of John the Baptist or are the evangelist's own reflection; many modern translations close the Baptist's words at v. 30. Either way, they sum up the themes of chapter 3: above and below, testimony, the Spirit, the Son, and eternal life.
str: v. 31: the one from above and the one from the earth.
vv. 32–33: his testimony, refused by many, accepted by some.
vv. 34–35: the Son speaks God's words; the Spirit without measure; all things in his hands.
v. 36: the decision: believe and have life, or disobey and not see life.
kw: The same word Jesus used to Nicodemus: to be born “from above” (3:3, 7). Only one who comes from above can give birth from above.
To put one's seal on a document, confirming it as true. Whoever believes sets his seal to God's truthfulness.

The Greek can mean that God gives the Spirit to the Son without measure, or that the Son gives the Spirit without measure; both are true. The prophets received the Spirit for a task; the Son has the Spirit in fullness.
vv: He whom God has sent speaks the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure.
The Father loves the Son and has placed all things in his hands.
All things: the world, judgment, life. The same hands will be stretched out on the Cross.
Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life
“Has”, in the present: eternal life begins now, in faith. The opposite of believing is “disobeying”: in John, faith is not just an opinion but obedience.
ch: The Catechism quotes 3:36 to teach that believing in Jesus Christ and in the One who sent him is necessary for salvation (CCC 161), and 3:34 to show that Jesus' whole life and mission are carried out in total communion with the Spirit whom the Father gives him “without measure” (CCC 1286). The God who sends his Son is a Father who loves: in John, judgment is light refused, not love withheld.

study: Paul boasts only of his weaknesses. Which weakness of mine could become the place where Christ's power is seen?
John says that eternal life begins with believing in the Son. What would change today if I truly lived as one who “has” eternal life?

lead: The Bible ends where it began, in a garden with a river and the tree of life. In the new Jerusalem God's servants worship him and see his face. The Gospel shows the way in: Jesus welcomes the little children, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these. Those who come to him like children are the ones who will see God's face.

r.h: They will see his face
set: This is the last vision of Revelation, the end of the description of the new Jerusalem coming down from heaven (21:1–22:5). John gathers images from the whole Bible: the river of Eden (Genesis 2:10); the river flowing from the Temple in Ezekiel's vision, with trees whose leaves are for healing (Ezekiel 47:1–12); and the tree of life, guarded after the fall (Genesis 3:22–24).
str: vv. 1–2: the river of the water of life and the tree of life.
v. 3a: nothing accursed any more.
vv. 3b–4: the throne, the worship, the face, the name.
v. 5: no more night; the Lord God is their light, and they reign for ever.
kw: The living water Jesus promised (John 4:14; 7:37–39); John explains that he spoke of the Spirit.
Barred to Adam and Eve after the fall, now open again. The Fathers often saw the Cross as the new tree of life.
The curse of Genesis 3:17 is lifted. Nothing will stand between God and his people again.
vv: Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb
One throne for God and the Lamb: the risen Christ shares the Father's throne.
Nothing accursed will be found there any more.
they will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads.

What Moses was refused (Exodus 33:20) is given to all God's servants. The name on the forehead recalls the gold plate on the high priest's turban, engraved “Holy to the Lord” (Exodus 28:36–38): all the redeemed are priests.
ch: The Catechism calls this contemplation of God in heavenly glory the beatific vision (CCC 1028), and sees in “the river of the water of life” one of the most beautiful symbols of the Holy Spirit, in the heavenly liturgy in which the Church on earth already shares (CCC 1137). Every Holy Qurbana is a sharing in the worship of “his servants” before the throne of God and of the Lamb.

r.h: Let the little children come to me
set: In Matthew this scene stands between Jesus' teaching on marriage (19:3–12) and the rich young man (19:16–22). It was a custom to ask a respected teacher to bless children. The disciples think the Teacher has more important work to do.
str: v. 13: children are brought for the laying on of hands and prayer; the disciples rebuke those who bring them.
v. 14: Jesus' answer.
kw: Small children, with no status or merit in that society. They bring nothing but their need.
The kingdom belongs not only to children but to all who receive it as children do: as a gift.
vv: Then little children were being brought to him in order that he might lay his hands on them and pray.
The laying on of hands is a gesture of blessing (Genesis 48:14). Matthew says that Jesus did so before he went on his way (19:15).
Let the little children come to me, and do not stop them; for it is to such as these that the kingdom of heaven belongs.
Mark adds that Jesus was indignant with the disciples and took the children up in his arms (Mark 10:14, 16).
ch: The Catechism teaches that to become a child in relation to God is the condition for entering the Kingdom (CCC 526). Jesus' tenderness toward children, shown in these words, is one reason for the Church's practice of baptizing infants and for her hope for children who die without baptism (CCC 1250, 1261).

study: Revelation promises that God's servants “will see his face”. How does this hope change the way I face death and loss?
What would it mean for me this week to receive the kingdom like the little children Jesus welcomed?

lead: On the third Sunday of Qudash Edtha the Church, the house of God, looks at the work of her members. All four readings are about labour done for someone. Jacob serves fourteen years for the woman he loves. Ben Sira tells the believer to stay at his task and trust the Lord for the result. Paul tells the Thessalonians to work quietly and earn their bread, as he himself did. In the Gospel, the master entrusts his property to his servants and returns to ask what they have done with it. The key words are service, faithfulness and accounting: what we do with what has been given to us, and for whom we do it.

r.h: Seven years that seemed a few days
set: Jacob has fled from his brother Esau after taking the blessing of the firstborn by deceit (Genesis 27). On the way he saw the ladder at Bethel and received God's promise (28:10–22). Now he has reached Haran, the home of his mother's brother Laban, and met Rachel at the well (29:1–14). He came with nothing in his hands; all he can offer is his work.

Marriage customs of the time help us read the story. A bridegroom normally gave a bride-price to the bride's family. Jacob has no money, so he offers years of labour instead. The bride came to the bridegroom veiled, and the marriage was celebrated with a feast of seven days (compare Judges 14:12).
str: vv. 15–20: Laban asks about wages; Jacob offers seven years for Rachel; the years pass “but a few days” because of love.
vv. 21–25: the wedding feast; in the evening Laban brings Leah; in the morning Jacob discovers the deception.
vv. 26–28: Laban's excuse (the custom of the land) and a new bargain: complete Leah's week and serve seven more years.
vv. 29–30: Rachel is given; Jacob loves her more than Leah and serves another seven years.

¶ The story is full of reversals. Jacob deceived his blind father in the dark to take the right of the firstborn; now in the dark he is given the firstborn instead of the younger. The deceiver is deceived. The Bible does not comment; it lets the reader see how God educates Jacob through what he suffers.
kw: The verb appears again and again in this chapter (vv. 15, 18, 20, 25, 27, 30). The same Hebrew root gives the words for servant, for labour and for the worship of God. Jacob's long service is the school in which the proud younger brother becomes a patient man.
From the same root as mirmâ, “deceit”, the word Isaac used of Jacob himself: “Your brother came deceitfully” (27:35). The echo is deliberate: Jacob tastes what he once did to others.

The Hebrew word can mean soft, tender or weak, so translations differ. The NRSV says Leah's eyes were “lovely”; the Malayalam POC says they were dim (മങ്ങിയവ). The verse contrasts the two sisters, but Scripture goes on to honour Leah: from her come Levi and Judah, the priestly tribe and the royal tribe of David.
vv: So Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him but a few days because of the love he had for her.
One of the most beautiful sentences in Genesis. Love does not shorten the years; it changes how they are lived. Work done for someone we love does not feel like slavery.
What is this you have done to me? Did I not serve with you for Rachel? Why then have you deceived me?
Jacob's protest sounds like Esau's cry in chapter 27. The man who cheated now knows how it feels. God does not approve Laban's fraud, but he uses it to humble and mature Jacob.
and he loved Rachel more than Leah. He served Laban for another seven years.
The story does not hide the pain of an unequal love, and the next verse says that the Lord saw that Leah was unloved (29:31). God's care goes to the one who is overlooked.
ch: Many Fathers read this story as a figure of Christ. St Justin Martyr, in his Dialogue with Trypho, says that Jacob served Laban for both daughters, and that Christ also serves for all whom he wishes to gather (in substance). St Augustine, in his work Against Faustus, saw in Leah, whose name he linked with labour, the active life of work and service, and in Rachel the contemplative life of seeing God; the believer must accept Leah first in order to reach Rachel (in substance). On this Sunday the story teaches that faithful work, even long and hidden, is the way God forms his servants.

r.h: Grow old in your work
set: The Book of Sirach was written in Hebrew in Jerusalem around 180 BC by Jesus son of Eleazar son of Sira, a teacher of wisdom. His grandson translated it into Greek in Egypt some fifty years later, as he tells us in his prologue. The Church received it among the inspired books; its Latin name Ecclesiasticus means “the Church's book”, because it was used so much to teach the faith and good conduct.
Chapter 11 speaks about trust in God against appearances. A poor man may be wise, a rich man may lose everything, and the sinner's success is no reason for envy.
str: v. 20: stand by your task and grow old in it.
vv. 21–22: do not envy the sinner; trust the Lord, who can change a poor man's lot in a moment.
vv. 23–24: two false sayings: “What do I need?” and “I have enough.”
vv. 25–27: good days and bad days make us forget each other; the end of a life shows what it truly was.
kw: The Greek word normally means “covenant”. Here it means the duty or charge a person has accepted. Faithfulness in daily work is a kind of covenant faithfulness.
Ben Sira honours ordinary work. To “grow old in your work” is not a curse but a blessing: a life spent steadily at an honest task.
The reward of the devout is not first of all money but God's blessing, which can “flourish” quickly when God wills.
vv: Stand by your agreement and attend to it, and grow old in your work.
Perseverance is the first virtue of the worker. Many begin well; the wise man stays.
trust in the Lord and keep at your job; for it is easy in the sight of the Lord to make the poor rich suddenly, in an instant.
Trust and work go together. We do the work; God gives the increase.
at the close of one’s life one’s deeds are revealed.

Ben Sira does not yet speak clearly of life after death, but he knows that the truth of a life appears at its end. The New Testament will bring this to full light in the judgment of Christ, as today's Gospel shows.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that by their work people provide for themselves and their families, serve their neighbours and share in the work of the Creator (Gaudium et Spes 34 and 67). Ben Sira's advice to “grow old in your work” is the Old Testament form of this teaching. The two false sayings of vv. 23–24 warn against the self-sufficiency that Jesus will condemn in the rich fool (Luke 12:16–21).

r.h: Work quietly and earn your bread
set: Thessalonica was the chief city of Macedonia, a busy port. Paul founded the Church there on his second missionary journey (Acts 17:1–9) and had to leave quickly. In this letter he corrects some who were saying that “the day of the Lord is already here” (2:2). It seems that some members had stopped working, perhaps because they thought the end was near, perhaps because they preferred to live on the generosity of others.
Paul himself worked with his hands as a tentmaker (Acts 18:3) so as not to be a burden on the young Churches (1 Thessalonians 2:9).
str: v. 6: keep away from those who live in idleness, against the tradition received.
vv. 7–9: Paul's own example: he worked night and day, though he had the right to be supported.
v. 10: the rule: “Anyone unwilling to work should not eat.”
vv. 11–12: some are busybodies, not doing any work; they must work quietly.
vv. 13–15: do not grow tired of doing good; correct the disobedient as brothers, not enemies.
kw: Originally a military word for a soldier who leaves the ranks. The problem is not only laziness but disorder in the community.
A play on words in Greek: “not busy working, but busy with what is not their business”. Idleness easily turns into interference in other people's lives.
What Paul handed on to them: not only teaching but also a way of living. Christian tradition includes the example of ordinary honest work.
vv: Anyone unwilling to work should not eat.
Paul speaks of those who are unwilling, not of those who are unable. The sick, the old and the poor who cannot work are always the Church's care.
Brothers and sisters, do not be weary in doing what is right.
After the warning, encouragement. Doing good over a long time is tiring; the community needs to support one another.
Do not regard them as enemies, but warn them as believers.
Even the discipline of the Church is meant to heal and bring back. The one who is corrected remains a brother.
ch: The Catechism quotes this very verse: “Hence work is a duty: ‘If any one will not work, let him not eat’” (CCC 2427, citing 2 Thessalonians 3:10). It adds that work honours the Creator's gifts and that it can be a means of sanctification when united with Christ. St John Paul II, in his encyclical Laborem Exercens (1981), developed this teaching, calling work a key to the whole social question. The early Christian handbook called the Didache (ch. 12) already told communities that a visiting Christian who wished to settle among them should work for his bread and not live idle at their expense (in substance).

r.h: Faithful in a few things
set: This is the second of the three closing parables of Jesus' last discourse (Matthew 24–25). The ten bridesmaids teach readiness; the talents teach faithful work while the master is away; the judgment of the nations teaches love for the least. All three answer one question: how should disciples live during the time between Jesus' going and his coming?

A talent was not a coin but a very large weight of silver, about six thousand denarii. Since a denarius was a labourer's daily wage, one talent was the wages of many years. Even the servant who received “only” one talent received a fortune. Later Jewish law held that a man who buried entrusted money was no longer responsible if it was stolen, so the third servant thought he was being careful.
str: vv. 14–15: the master entrusts his property, “to each according to his ability”, and goes away.
vv. 16–18: two servants trade and double the money; the third digs a hole and hides it.
vv. 19–23: “after a long time” the master returns; the first two receive the same praise.
vv. 24–25: the third servant's speech: “I knew that you were a harsh man… so I was afraid.”
vv. 26–30: the master's judgment; the talent is given to the one with ten.
kw: From this parable the word “talent” came to mean a natural ability in English and other languages. In the parable it stands for everything God entrusts: life, faith, gifts, time, the Gospel itself.
The same word as “believing”. Faith in Matthew is shown in faithfulness: doing the master's work while he is away.
The word means hesitating, shrinking back. The third servant's sin is not theft but fear that refuses to act.
vv: to one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one, to each according to his ability.
God does not give everyone the same gifts, and he does not ask the same results. He asks each person to use what he was given.
Well done, good and trustworthy slave; you have been trustworthy in a few things, I will put you in charge of many things; enter into the joy of your master.
The servant with two talents receives exactly the same praise (v. 23). What counts is faithfulness, not the amount. Five talents are called “a few things” compared with the joy that follows.
so I was afraid, and I went and hid your talent in the ground. Here you have what is yours.

The third servant's picture of his master is false, and his fear comes from that false picture. A person who sees God only as a harsh judge will bury his gifts. A person who knows God's generosity will dare to use them.
For to all those who have, more will be given, and they will have an abundance; but from those who have nothing, even what they have will be taken away.
Not a rule of economics but a law of the spiritual life: gifts that are used grow; gifts that are hidden are lost.
ch: St Gregory the Great, preaching on this parable, says that no one may say he has received nothing: everyone has at least one talent, and he must render an account of it (in substance). The Catechism teaches that talents are not distributed equally, and that these differences belong to God's plan, who wills that each receive what he needs from others and that those with particular talents share them (CCC 1936–1937). The parable describes the Church in the time of waiting: every baptised person has received the master's property and is asked to make it bear fruit.

qa: Does God approve of Laban's trick or Jacob's two wives?

No. Genesis tells the history of the patriarchs honestly, with their sins and the customs of their time. The deceit is shown as a wrong that brings pain. God works through imperfect people without approving all they do. The original plan of one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24) is restored by Jesus (Matthew 19:4–6).
Was the master in the parable really harsh?

No. That is how the frightened servant saw him. The master in fact entrusts huge sums, praises generously and shares his joy. Jesus uses the servant's own words to show that fear and a false image of God paralyse a person.
Does Paul's rule mean the unemployed should go hungry?
No. Paul speaks of those unwilling to work, who live on others while able to work. The Church has always cared for the sick, the aged and those who cannot find work (CCC 2427–2436).
rite: In Qudash Edtha the East Syriac tradition contemplates the Church as the house God has built and consecrated. A house is kept alive by the daily work of those who live in it. Today's readings remind the Syro-Malabar faithful that work in field, shop, office, home and parish is part of the Church's worship when it is offered with Christ in the Holy Qurbana. The many Syro-Malabar families who work far from home, in the Gulf and other lands, may see themselves in Jacob, labouring for years for those they love, and in the faithful servants who will hear “enter into the joy of your master”.
study: Jacob's years “seemed to him but a few days because of the love he had”. For whom do I work, and does love change the way I work?
Sirach warns against saying “I have enough”. Where am I tempted by self-sufficiency?
Paul worked with his hands to give an example. What example does my way of working give to my children or colleagues?
What “talent” have I buried out of fear, and what would it mean to trust the Master enough to use it?

lead: Today both readings ask what matters most. Paul tells the Corinthians, proud of their spectacular gifts, that without love even the greatest gifts are nothing. In the Gospel a scribe asks Jesus which commandment is first, and Jesus joins love of God and love of neighbour into one answer. The two readings explain each other: the “greatest gift” is the fulfilment of the “greatest commandment”.

r.h: Without love I am nothing
set: Corinth was a rich, mixed port city, and its young Church was divided. In chapters 12–14 Paul deals with spiritual gifts. Some Corinthians prized speaking in tongues above everything. Chapter 13 stands between the teaching on the body of Christ (ch. 12) and practical rules for worship (ch. 14). It is not a wedding poem first of all, but a correction of a gifted and quarrelsome community.
str: vv. 1–3: gifts without love: tongues, prophecy, knowledge, faith, even giving everything away, are worth nothing.
vv. 4–7: what love does and does not do: fifteen verbs describing love in action.
vv. 8–10: love never ends; the gifts are partial and will pass when the complete comes.
kw: The self-giving love that seeks the good of the other. Paul describes it not with adjectives but with verbs: love is something one does.
Literally “is long-tempered”: slow to anger, able to wait. The Greek Old Testament uses the same idea of God himself, “slow to anger” (Exodus 34:6).
What is whole and finished: the vision of God at the end. Then the partial gifts will no longer be needed, but love will remain.
vv: If I give away all my possessions, and if I hand over my body so that I may boast, but do not have love, I gain nothing.

A note on the text. The Greek manuscripts differ by one letter. Some of the oldest read “so that I may boast” (kauchēsōmai), which the NRSV follows. Others read “to be burned” (kauthēsomai), which the Latin Vulgate and the Malayalam POC follow (ദഹിപ്പിക്കാൻ). Either way the point is the same: even martyrdom without love would gain nothing.
Love is patient; love is kind; love is not envious or boastful or arrogant
St Paul could almost be describing Christ. Put the name of Jesus in place of “love” and the sentences remain true.
Love never ends.
ch: The Catechism quotes this chapter to describe charity, the greatest of the theological virtues, and calls it the “form” of all the virtues: it gives them life and order (CCC 1822–1827, quoting 1 Corinthians 13:1–7). St Thérèse of Lisieux, reading chapters 12 and 13, understood that her vocation in the heart of the Church was love (Story of a Soul, ms. B, in substance).

r.h: Not far from the kingdom of God
set: Jesus is teaching in the Temple in Jerusalem in the last days before his Passion. One group after another has questioned him to trap him. This scribe is different: he heard that Jesus “answered them well” and asks a sincere question. The teachers of the Law counted 613 commandments, and they did discuss which ones were weightier.
str: v. 28: the scribe's question.
vv. 29–31: Jesus' answer: the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4–5) and love of neighbour (Leviticus 19:18).
vv. 32–33: the scribe repeats and approves, adding that love is more than sacrifices.
v. 34: “You are not far from the kingdom of God.”
kw: The first word of Deuteronomy 6:4, the prayer devout Jews say morning and evening. Jesus begins with listening before loving.
Repeated four times: all your heart, soul, mind and strength. Love of God takes the whole person, not a part.
vv: you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength.
You shall love your neighbor as yourself.
Jesus was asked for one commandment and gave two. They cannot be separated: love of neighbour is the proof of love of God (compare 1 John 4:20).
You are not far from the kingdom of God.
The scribe understands; he is near. The one step left is to follow the one who is speaking to him. The Kingdom is not only a teaching but a person.
ch: The Catechism opens its teaching on the Ten Commandments with this answer of Jesus: the two great commandments sum up the whole Law (CCC 2055, 2196). This Gospel shows a moment of agreement between Jesus and a Jewish teacher on the heart of the Law, and the Church sees in it the common root she shares with the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4).

qa: Is 1 Corinthians 13 about marriage?
Paul wrote it for a whole community troubled by pride and division. It fits a wedding well, because marriage needs exactly this patient love, but it applies to every Christian relationship.
study: Read 1 Corinthians 13:4–7 and put your own name in place of “love”. Which line is hardest to say honestly?
The scribe was “not far” from the Kingdom. What one step separates me from following Christ more fully?

lead: One word links today's readings: steward. Paul calls the apostles “stewards of God’s mysteries” who must be found trustworthy. Jesus tells of a steward who was dishonest but shrewd, and draws the lesson: be faithful in little things and you will be trusted with true riches. In the season of the Church's dedication, every Christian is reminded that what he holds belongs to Another.

r.h: Stewards of God's mysteries
set: The Corinthians had formed parties around their favourite preachers: “I belong to Paul”, “I belong to Apollos” (1:12). They compared and judged their teachers. Paul answers that preachers are only servants, and that the only judge who matters is the Lord.
str: vv. 1–2: what apostles are: servants and stewards, who must be trustworthy.
vv. 3–4: Paul does not depend on human verdicts, not even on his own conscience; the Lord judges.
v. 5: do not judge before the time; the Lord will reveal the hidden purposes of the heart.
kw: An assistant who carries out the orders of another. The apostle does not act on his own authority.
The manager of a household, often himself a slave, who looked after his master's goods and gave each servant his portion. The same word appears in today's Gospel (Luke 16:1).
God's saving plan, once hidden and now revealed in Christ. In the Eastern Churches the word came to name the sacraments as well, the Holy Mysteries entrusted to the Church's ministers.
vv: Moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found trustworthy.
Not brilliant, not popular, but trustworthy. The steward's virtue is faithfulness to the master.
Then each one will receive commendation from God.
Paul ends with hope, not fear. The Lord's judgment will bring to light the hidden good as well as the hidden evil.
ch: The Second Vatican Council and the Catechism describe ordained ministers as servants of Christ who act in his person, not by their own power (CCC 875–876). The Fathers often applied this verse to bishops and priests as dispensers of the sacraments. Every baptised person is also a steward of the gifts of grace (1 Peter 4:10).

r.h: Faithful in a very little
set: Luke 16 is about the right use of wealth, and follows the parables of mercy in chapter 15. The parable of the dishonest steward is one of the hardest in the Gospels. A manager, about to be dismissed for wasting his master's goods, quickly reduces the debts of his master's debtors so that they will welcome him later. The master praises him, not for his dishonesty, but for acting shrewdly.
str: vv. 1–2: the steward is accused and dismissed.
vv. 3–4: his inner monologue: “What will I do?”
vv. 5–7: he reduces the debts.
v. 8: the master praises his shrewdness.
vv. 9–13: Jesus' sayings on wealth: make friends with it, be faithful in little, you cannot serve two masters.
kw: Prudently, with practical wisdom. The same word used of the wise bridesmaids (Matthew 25:2). Jesus wants his disciples to be as alert for the Kingdom as worldly people are for their own interests.
An Aramaic word for property or riches, perhaps from a root meaning “that in which one trusts”. Jesus speaks of wealth almost as a rival master.
The NRSV “jugs” and “containers” translate the Hebrew measures bath (for oil) and kor (for wheat), which the POC keeps (ബത്ത്, കോർ). The debts were very large.
vv: for the children of this age are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than are the children of light.

“Children of light” was a name some Jewish groups of the time used for the faithful, as the Dead Sea Scrolls show. Jesus' sad observation: worldly people often plan more carefully for this life than believers do for eternal life.
Whoever is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much; and whoever is dishonest in a very little is dishonest also in much.
Character is formed in small things: a little honesty, a little punctuality, a small promise kept.
You cannot serve God and wealth.
The verb is “serve as a slave”. One can use money; one cannot belong to it.
ch: The Catechism teaches that disordered love of money is a form of idolatry, quoting the Lord: “You cannot serve God and mammon” (CCC 2113). Many Fathers explained the “friends” of v. 9 as the poor, who will welcome the generous into the eternal homes; so St Augustine and St Ambrose (in substance). Wealth becomes holy when it is shared.

qa: Does Jesus praise dishonesty?

No. The master (and Jesus) praise the steward's quick, decisive prudence, not his fraud. Jesus calls him “dishonest” (v. 8). The lesson is: use present goods wisely and generously for the sake of eternal life.
study: What has God entrusted to me as a “steward”, and how would I give an account of it today?
In what small matter of honesty or faithfulness is God asking more of me this week?

lead: Both readings speak about belonging to God's Kingdom. Paul reminds the Corinthians, who were suing one another in pagan courts, that they have been washed and sanctified and must live as heirs of the Kingdom. Jesus tells the Pharisees, who loved money, that God knows the heart, and that since John the Baptist the Kingdom is being preached and people press to enter it. Entering the Kingdom is a gift received in baptism and an effort kept up every day.

r.h: You were washed, sanctified, justified
set: In Corinth some Christians were taking their quarrels about property and money before the city's civil courts, in front of pagan judges. Paul is shocked, not because courts are evil in themselves, but because brothers in Christ were exposing their divisions to outsiders instead of settling them in love within the Church.
str: vv. 1–6: why go before unbelievers? The saints will judge the world; find a wise brother to decide.
vv. 7–8: lawsuits among you are already a defeat; better to suffer wrong.
vv. 9–10: the unrighteous will not inherit the Kingdom: a list of sins that exclude from it.
v. 11: “this is what some of you used to be. But you were washed…”
kw: Paul's ordinary word for all baptised Christians: those set apart for God. Holiness is first God's gift, then a task.
A clear reference to baptism. The three verbs, washed, sanctified, justified, all describe what God has already done.
The Kingdom is an inheritance: received as children, not earned as wages, but it can be lost by refusing to live as children.
vv: In fact, to have lawsuits at all with one another is already a defeat for you. Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be defrauded?
Paul echoes the teaching of Jesus about turning the other cheek (Matthew 5:39–40). A community that wins its lawsuits but loses its love has already lost.
And this is what some of you used to be. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God.
After a hard list of sins comes this great “But”. No one is beyond the reach of grace. The verse also names the Father (“our God”), the Son and the Spirit: baptism is the work of the whole Trinity.
ch: The Catechism quotes 1 Corinthians 6:11 at the opening of its teaching on life in Christ and again on the sacrament of reconciliation: we must appreciate the greatness of the gift God has given in the sacraments of Christian initiation, and Penance is offered to those who after baptism have fallen into sin (CCC 1425, 1695). The Church's own way of settling disputes, through the bishop and the ecclesiastical tribunals, grew partly from this chapter.

r.h: God knows your hearts
set: These verses follow the parable of the dishonest steward. Jesus' saying that no one can serve God and wealth provokes scorn from some Pharisees. Luke describes them as “lovers of money”. This is Luke's picture of particular opponents in a particular scene, not a judgement on all Pharisees, many of whom were sincere and devout teachers of the Law.
str: v. 13: no one can serve two masters.
vv. 14–15: some Pharisees ridicule him; God knows the heart.
v. 16: the Law and the prophets until John; now the Kingdom is preached.
v. 17: yet not one stroke of the Law will fall.
kw: Literally “turned up their noses”. Scorn is the defence of a heart that does not want to change.
tries to enter it by force (v. 16)

A difficult word: it can mean to use force or to press in urgently. Here it describes the eagerness of those who respond to the Gospel, like the tax collectors and sinners of Luke 15. The Kingdom requires decision and effort.
A tiny hook or stroke that distinguishes one Hebrew letter from another. The Law is not abolished by Jesus but fulfilled.
vv: but God knows your hearts; for what is prized by human beings is an abomination in the sight of God.
Human honour and divine judgment often differ. God looks at the heart (1 Samuel 16:7).
The law and the prophets were in effect until John came; since then the good news of the kingdom of God is proclaimed, and everyone tries to enter it by force.
For Luke, John the Baptist stands at the turning point of history: he closes the time of promise and opens the time of fulfilment.
But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away, than for one stroke of a letter in the law to be dropped.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus did not abolish the Law but fulfilled it, quoting the Lord's words on the smallest letter and stroke (CCC 577–582). The Church honours the Old Testament as true word of God and never set it aside (CCC 121–123). St Ambrose and other Fathers read v. 16 as a description of the holy effort of faith: the Kingdom is taken not by violence against others, but by the strength of a converted heart (in substance).

study: Is there a quarrel in my family or parish that I am trying to win rather than to heal?
“God knows your hearts.” What would change if I cared more for God's view of me than for the opinion of others?

lead: Fruit is the word of the day. Paul thanks God that the Gospel is “bearing fruit and growing” among the Colossians and prays that they may “bear fruit in every good work”. In the Gospel Jesus explains why he speaks in parables and interprets the parable of the sower: the seed is the same, the soil makes the difference. The seed bears fruit in the one who hears the word and understands it.

r.h: Bearing fruit and growing
set: Colossae was a small town in the Lycus valley in Asia Minor (modern Turkey). Paul had not founded this Church himself; it was founded by Epaphras, his co-worker (1:7). Paul writes from prison, to strengthen the Colossians against teachings that were drawing them away from Christ's supremacy. The letter begins, as usual, with thanksgiving and prayer.
str: vv. 3–8: thanksgiving for their faith, love and hope, and for the Gospel bearing fruit since Epaphras taught them.
vv. 9–11: Paul's prayer: knowledge of God's will, a worthy life, fruit in good works, strength and patience.
kw: The three theological virtues appear together, as in 1 Corinthians 13:13 and 1 Thessalonians 1:3. Here hope is “laid up for you in heaven”, like a treasure kept safe.
These words recall God's first blessing in Genesis 1:28, “Be fruitful and multiply”. The Gospel brings about a new creation.
Not mere information but deep, personal knowledge of God, which shows itself in a way of life.
vv: Just as it is bearing fruit and growing in the whole world, so it has been bearing fruit among yourselves from the day you heard it and truly comprehended the grace of God.
so that you may lead lives worthy of the Lord, fully pleasing to him, as you bear fruit in every good work and as you grow in the knowledge of God.
Knowledge and good works grow together. Knowing God leads to good works, and doing good leads to knowing God better.
ch: The Catechism teaches that faith, hope and charity are the foundation of Christian moral life, infused by God to make us capable of acting as his children (CCC 1812–1813). Paul's prayer for the Colossians is a model of intercession: he thanks God first, then asks for wisdom and perseverance for others (CCC 2634–2638, in substance).

r.h: The seed on good soil
set: Matthew 13 is the third of the five great discourses in Matthew's Gospel, a chapter of seven parables of the Kingdom. Jesus has just told the parable of the sower to the crowds from a boat (13:1–9). Now the disciples ask why he teaches this way. Opposition to Jesus has grown (ch. 11–12), and the parables both reveal and conceal: they open the Kingdom to those who are willing to come close and ask.
str: vv. 10–17: why parables: to you it has been given to know; the prophecy of Isaiah 6:9–10; blessed are your eyes.
vv. 18–23: the explanation of the sower: the path, the rocky ground, the thorns, the good soil.
kw: The hidden plan of God now revealed in Jesus. It is “given”: understanding the Kingdom is a gift.
A key word in Matthew 13. The good soil is the one who “hears the word and understands it”. Understanding in the Bible involves the heart and leads to obedience.
Literally “stumbles”. Trouble and persecution become a stumbling block for one without roots.
vv: But blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear.
The disciples are not cleverer than others; they are blessed because they stay with Jesus and ask him.
But as for what was sown on good soil, this is the one who hears the word and understands it, who indeed bears fruit and yields, in one case a hundredfold, in another sixty, and in another thirty.
Even the good soil gives different harvests. God does not ask the same yield from everyone, but he asks for fruit.
ch: A note on the text. Mark says Jesus speaks in parables “in order that” they may look but not perceive (Mark 4:12); Matthew says “because” they do not perceive (13:13). Matthew stresses the people's own closed hearts. The Catechism says that the parables are like mirrors: will a person be hard soil or good earth? Through them Jesus invites people to the feast of the Kingdom, but he also asks for a radical choice (CCC 546).

qa: Does Jesus speak in parables to keep people out?
No. Parables call for a response. Those who come close and ask, like the disciples, receive the explanation. The closed heart, not God's wish, keeps a person outside (Matthew 13:15; 1 Timothy 2:4).
study: Which soil best describes my hearing of the word this past week: path, rock, thorns or good soil?
Paul thanks God for the faith of others. Whose faith can I thank God for today?

lead: Both readings speak of God at work on his children to make them fruitful. Hebrews compares the trials of believers to a father's discipline, which “yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness”. In John, the Father is the vinegrower who prunes the branches so that they bear more fruit. The pruning hurts, but its purpose is life, and the condition for fruit is to abide in Christ.

r.h: The Lord disciplines those whom he loves
set: Chapter 11 of Hebrews listed the heroes of faith; chapter 12 opens by telling the readers to run their race looking to Jesus, who endured the cross (12:1–3). The readers have suffered public abuse and loss of property (10:32–34), but not yet bloodshed. The author helps them see their hardships not as signs that God has abandoned them, but as the training of sons and daughters.
str: v. 4: you have not yet resisted to the point of blood.
vv. 5–6: a quotation from Proverbs 3:11–12: the Lord disciplines those he loves.
vv. 7–11: the argument from human fathers to the Father of spirits; discipline is painful now but fruitful later.
